items.title: Home
items.text:
mibz2 decodes bzip2. It is block-parallel, as lbzip2 is. Within a block, its inverse BWT is walked as 32 interleaved chains, so a core keeps many of the walk's cache-missing loads in flight instead of one.

Think of a courier who learns each address only on arriving at the last one: the bike is fast, but most of the time goes on waiting to find out where to go next. That is the ordinary inverse BWT. mibz2 runs 32 such delivery chains through one dispatch centre, so while one waits for its next address, the others move. None of them travels faster; the waits overlap. Why 32 couriers beat one explains the idea, where it stops paying, and what has been measured.

  • Its output is byte for byte libbzip2's, and every block CRC and stream CRC is checked.
  • It runs on any x86-64 or aarch64 CPU. Its SIMD kernels (AVX2, PCLMULQDQ) are chosen at run time, and each has a portable scalar twin.
  • The library depends on std only.
>>> import mibz2
>>> data = mibz2.decompress(open("file.bz2", "rb").read())
>>> data[:18]
b'line one\nline two\n'
>>> with mibz2.open("file.bz2") as f:
...     lines = f.readlines()
...     verified = f.raw.verified
>>> len(lines), verified
(2000, True)

Its name is for "multi-chain inversion of bzip2". It was written in wikidata-pq, to decode the Wikidata dump, and knows nothing of Wikidata (history).

items.title: History
items.text:
• In wikidata-pq. mibz2 was written in lmmx/wikidata-pq, whose split decodes the Wikidata JSON dump. A profile there found the bz2 decode about half of the split's CPU, bound by the inverse BWT's chain of dependent loads, and a prototype walked it as interleaved chains (lmmx/wikidata-pq#194). The production decoder followed behind a flag (WIKIDATA_BZ2_DECODER=native, lmmx/wikidata-pq#197): on CI, the split's CPU fell 20.6% and its wall 16.6% against lbzip2.
  • The bake-off. Before going further, it was timed against pbz2, fbz, the lbzip2 crate, indexed_bzip2, lbzip2 and libbzip2 on the dump's blocks. pbz2 0.2.0 tied it; the others were 1.5–1.9× slower at 4 threads (lmmx/wikidata-pq#199).
  • Its own repository. The decoder's history moved to lmmx/mibz2 by git filter-repo, its paths renamed and each #N in its commit messages rewritten to lmmx/wikidata-pq#N, with its journals. It was published as 0.1.0 and 0.1.1 on crates.io and PyPI, the crate and the Python package at one version.

The journals record each step, and Status says where the research stands now.

items.title: Status
items.text:
As of 29 October 2026. This page is a snapshot of where the research stands. The evidence is in the journals and the pull requests linked below.

In short: - A faster way to run the inverse BWT on a many-core machine has been found, confirmed and explained. - It is not in the released decoder yet. mibz2 0.1.5 decodes as it did, and every figure here is the inversion stage alone, not whole decompression.

items.title: The starting point: a knee at four workers
items.text:
• mibz2's decoder gives each worker its own block. The inverse BWT then walks that block's table: about 3.6 MB for a full 900 kB block, one random load per output byte.
  • On a 10-core i9-10900K, with a 20 MB shared L3, throughput peaks at 4 workers and falls beyond them. Eight tables don't fit in the L3, and the walk's loads go to DRAM.

items.title: The finding: cooperative inversion
items.text:
Several cores share one block's table: the table is built together and walked together, each core taking segments of the walk from a shared counter. An arm is written Nxk: N blocks in flight, k cores on each. Production's independent workers are p4, p8 and so on.

Measured on the i9 in the research harness (PR #73):

arm what runs inversion MB/s against p4 (paired, 95% interval) p4 production, 4 independent workers 1,465 1 p8 production, 8 independent workers 662 0.47 4x2 4 blocks, 2 cores each 1,808 1.230 (1.217–1.243) 3x3 3 blocks, 3 cores each (9 cores) 1,942 1.323 (1.312–1.335) s3x3 libsais 2.12.1, 3 blocks on 3 threads each 2,355 1.59
  • The confirmation was registered before the runs.
  • 4x2 and 3x3 were each run alone against p4, 20 paired rounds each.
  • Each beat p4 in all 20 rounds, and every block's output was checked.
  • 4x2 reproduced its discovery figure within 0.3%.
  • 3x3 came in 2.3% under its discovery figure, as picking the best of 19 arms would predict.
  • libsais's inverse BWT is still about 20% ahead at 3x3 (1.195× ours, paired). It gains from cooperation by the same factor as ours, about 1.5×. The gap between them is the kernel.

items.title: Why it works: two mechanisms, measured
items.text:
A hardware-counter study on the same machine ran each arm alone under perf stat, with counters that include the walk's software prefetches. It was 588 runs, none multiplexed (PR #84).

arm L3 hit share of data reads past L2 reads in flight, machine-wide wait per read p4 94.5% 28.1 67 cycles p8 65.7% 70.0 366 cycles 4x2 94.9% 38.8 64 cycles 3x3 96.7% 41.9 66 cycles
  • Residency.
  • With eight cores either way, four shared tables (4x2) stay in the L3 where eight independent ones (p8) don't. The hit share rises from 66% to 95%, and each read waits 64 cycles instead of 366.
  • Overlap.
  • With four tables either way, the second core on each (4x2 against p4) leaves the hit share and the wait unchanged.
  • It puts 1.38× as many reads in flight.
  • 3x3 has both: a higher hit share than p4, a third fewer reads missing the L3 per byte, and 1.49× the reads in flight.
  • The counters account for the timings. Little's law on them (reads in flight over the wait, against reads per byte) reproduces each arm's measured throughput to within 0–11%.

items.title: What it points at
items.text:
The cooperative kernel retires more instructions per output byte than production's or libsais's:

kernel instructions per output byte production (p4) 23.8 cooperative, one core a block (4x1) 31.8 cooperative, 3x3 35.3 libsais, one core a block (s4x1) 21.4 libsais, 3x3 23.2
  • Its 4x1 penalty is instructions, not memory.
  • The cooperative kernel on one core a block (4x1) runs at 0.87× production.
  • Its reads and waits are within 10% of production's; it executes a third more instructions.
  • libsais's lead is fewer reads.
  • It makes 0.86–0.89 reads past L2 per byte, against our 1.40–1.55. That is one dependent load for two output bytes.
  • It does so within about 23 instructions a byte.
  • mibz2's own two-byte walk (#6) wins only past the knee. At its best it reaches 0.86× the one-byte walk's best.

items.title: What's next
items.text:
order work what it is for 1 #77: the cooperative kernel's instructions, attributed to code by perf annotate (PR #85) before any change production's instructions a byte, and production's speed at one core a block 2 #78, #81: the build's recount and extra pass a cheaper shared build: 43% of 3x3's time 3 #79: a smaller table more teams resident at once (a scheduling gain, not one for 3x3 itself) later a two-byte walk within production's instruction budget libsais's fewer reads a byte

Still open in the counter record: - 3 short checks of the raw L3 event's accounting, with their criteria fixed in advance. It counts a steady 23–39% more requests than offcore_requests.all_data_rd, and the likely cause is prefetches into L3. - The study's conclusions rest on the arm-to-arm directions, which a second, independent pair of counters reproduces.

Before any of this reaches a release: - the cooperative build and walk must pass the decoder's correctness checks: the segment oracle, fuzzing and Miri on the shared table; - the whole decoder must be A/B'd at 4–10 cores, where an inversion-stage gain counts only as far as it survives; - other CPUs must be measured too. CI's 4-core runners can't show a gain that only exists past four workers, so the workstation measures it.

items.title: Benchmarks
items.text:
mibz2's speed is measured on GitHub's runners by the Benchmark workflow (.github/workflows/bench.yml), with the A/B harness examples/ab.rs and bench/report.py. Nothing about performance is decided on a developer's machine.

  • History: master's figures over its commits.
  • Alternatives: the latest master commit against the other bzip2 decoders: pbz2, lbzip2, indexed_bzip2, fbz, the lbzip2 crate, libbzip2 and libbz2-rs.

These are decoder-level results: one process decoding one file, nothing else. End-to-end results, the decoder inside a pipeline, are in wikidata-pq's benchmark history.

items.title: What runs when
items.text:
event arms result a pull request that touches the decoder, the harness, the corpora or the bench its head and its base (the merge base with master), both built on the runner one comment on the pull request, edited in place on every push a push to master mibz2 and the alternatives the commit's result on the bench-results branch, and these pages the Actions tab either: a base commit given, as a pull request; none, as master the run's summary, not recorded

Pull requests never run the alternatives: their runs are the head against the base only. The alternatives that are Rust crates with dependencies of their own (fbz, the lbzip2 crate, libbz2-rs) are built into a second build of the harness, bench/alternatives, so the crate's own dev-dependencies stay as they are.

Only master's commits are recorded. A pull request's runs, and experiments that did not land, are not recorded or shown here; experiments are written up in the journals.

items.title: The workload
items.text:
• The crate's corpora (ab gen, tests/common/mod.rs), at scale 4, each compressed by libbzip2 1.0.8 at level 9: text (the crate's own sources and README, repeated: 12 MB), random (8 MB), onebyte (one byte repeated, 20 MB), pattern (a 7-byte pattern, 19.6 MB), runs (runs of random lengths, 10 MB) and records (binary records, 9.6 MB). The text corpus is made from the commit's own sources, so its bytes change a little from commit to commit.
  • The Wikidata dump's own blocks: 12 byte-range windows of 1 MiB of wikidata-20261019-all.json.bz2, at (2i + 1)/24 of the file. examples/windows.rs keeps each window's whole blocks, their bits untouched, as a stream of its own, checked against libbzip2 and lbzip2: 431 blocks, 11.85 MB of bz2 → 209.7 MB of JSON (17.69×). bench/wikidata.json pins each window's offset, length and SHA-256, and the corpus's. Wikimedia serves a dated dump for about six weeks, so the windows are kept on the repository's bench-data branch.

items.title: How it is measured
items.text:
• A run is one process decoding one file from disk, end to end, its output hashed (the same hash for every arm, or the run fails: the same-bytes check). It records the wall time, the CPU time (user + sys), the peak RSS, and each thread's CPU.
  • A round decodes every corpus once with each arm at each thread count: 1 thread (pinned to one CPU) and the runner's cores. The arms' order is rotated and reversed round to round. There are 10 rounds.
  • Block-parallel or single-threaded: each arm is classed in its records (parallel). A single-threaded decoder (libbzip2, libbz2-rs) runs at 1 thread only, once a round; at the runner's cores its figures are those 1-thread runs, paired with mibz2's at that count, and shown as 1-thread runs, never as a decode on more threads.
  • On a pull request, the base's own harness binary is an arm (mibz2@base/ab), so both builds run in the same process shape on the same runner.
  • Paired ratios: each round's ratio of one arm's time to the reference arm's (the base; or mibz2, against the alternatives), their geometric mean, and its 95% t-interval over the rounds. A change is called faster or slower only where the interval excludes no change.
  • The bench version (bench/report.py, semver) is stamped on every result. A change to what is measured or how is a new major version, and the history never joins a series across major versions, runner CPU models or sets of corpora.

items.title: The full-dump figure is modelled
items.text:
Each result also gives a whole dump's decode (103.5 GB of bz2), modelled, not measured, from the Wikidata blocks' runs, round by round:

  • the scanner's time (the one serial thread: each block's header and Huffman symbols) per byte of bz2, scaled by the dump's bz2 bytes;
  • the workers' time per byte of output, scaled by the dump's output, taken as its bz2 bytes times the sample's ratio (17.69×; another sample of the same dump, 24 windows of 25 MB, measured 18.68×; wikidata-pq's CI slice, lines recompressed, is 13.69×);
  • at N threads, the larger of the scanner's time and the workers' over N, times the sample's own wall over that bound; the same gap read as a fixed cost is given beside it.

It assumes time linear in bytes, the sample's mix standing for the dump's, and the runner's CPU; its interval carries the rounds' spread and the sample ratio's.

items.title: Resources: CPU per byte and scaling, the wikidata corpus
items.text:
CPU per byte is the process's CPU (every thread, user + sys) over the output. Amplification is that at N threads over the same build's at 1, paired by round: 1× is no extra CPU for the same bytes, and above it the work costs more as threads are added (stalls, sharing, synchronisation; CPU counts a thread stalled on memory as running). Efficiency is the speedup over N. Run-queue is the threads' mean count runnable but not running.

threads: placement mibz2 MB/s mibz2 CPU ns/B mibz2 amplification mibz2 efficiency lbzip2 amplification pbz2 amplification 1: pinned to CPU 1 278 3.60 1 – 1 1 2: CPUs 0,2, one a core 424 3.93 1.09× (1.08–1.10) 76% 1.01× (1.01–1.02) 1.03× (1.03–1.03) 4: all 4 CPUs, sharing SMT siblings 533 6.25 1.73× (1.71–1.75) 48% 1.21× (1.21–1.22) 1.63× (1.61–1.65)

Best: mibz2 at 4 threads (533 MB/s); lbzip2 at 4 threads (196 MB/s); pbz2 at 4 threads (303 MB/s).

Conditions: 4 CPUs on 2 physical cores (0,1 | 2,3); no CPU quota; the run-queue counter checked and counting; 2-thread runs on CPUs 0,2 (one CPU a core); 4-thread runs share cores' SMT siblings.

How to read it, and what it cannot show - **The four comparisons the assessment reads,** declared in bench/report.py (`assessment`): best against best (wall), CPU per byte at the most threads, amplification at each thread count, and peak RSS at the most threads. Each moves only where its 95% interval excludes no change. With no real change, about one run in five flags one by chance: a flag that matters reproduces on a re-run. - **A trade-off is not a failure.** Faster for more CPU or memory, or the reverse, is for the reviewer to weigh against the deployment; the report names it, and nothing here fails CI but the outputs and the accounting. - **What it can't show:** which shared resource a rise in amplification comes from (cache, memory bandwidth, SMT, the scanner's handoffs): no hardware counters are read. CI's runners have 2 physical cores, so it cannot show a knee past 2 (the workstation's is at 4-5 workers, #39). The cores' L3 is shared with other tenants and its size unknown. - **Run-queue wait** (threads' mean count runnable, not running; schedstat): mibz2 1t 0.00, mibz2 2t 0.72, mibz2 4t 0.94, lbzip2 1t 0.09, lbzip2 2t 0.30, lbzip2 4t 0.56, pbz2 1t 0.00, pbz2 2t 0.35, pbz2 4t 0.39. A pinned 2-thread run has four threads (two workers, the scanner, the reader) on two CPUs, so some wait is its shape, not interference. - **The per-thread split's unattributed CPU** (the process's total that no sampled thread holds, sampled every 10 ms): mibz2 2t 7%, mibz2 4t 5%, lbzip2 2t 4%, lbzip2 4t 6%, pbz2 2t 4%, pbz2 4t 4%.

items.title: Modelled, not measured: a whole dump
items.text:
The decode of wikidata-20261019-all.json.bz2 (103 GB of bz2; 1.83 TB of JSON at the sample's 17.69×), scaled from the Wikidata blocks' runs above, round by round (mean ± its 95% interval, the sample ratio's own uncertainty added in):

mibz2 1 thread 1h50m ± 13m11s 4 threads 57m26s ± 8m04s 4 threads, the sample's overlap gap as a fixed cost 40m05s ± 5m38s the scanner alone (its serial part) 16m18s ± 26.3s the workers alone, over 4 40m05s ± 5m38s

At 4 threads the workers bound it. Per byte: the scanner 9.4 ns a byte of bz2, the workers 5.25 ns a byte of output at 4 threads (CPU, summed over them), 3.08 ns at 1 thread (wall, less the scanner's part); the scanner would bind from about 10 worker threads (mibz2).

What the model assumes - **Linear in bytes:** the scanner's time in the dump's bz2 bytes, the workers' in its output bytes. - **The sample stands for the dump:** 12 windows of 1 MiB at (2i + 1)/24 of the dump, 431 of its own blocks; their mix of entities and their ratio, 17.69× (the windows' 95% interval ±14.0%), stand for the whole dump's. Another sample of the same dump (wikidata-pq's bench/full, 24 windows of 25 MB) measured 18.68×; wikidata-pq's CI slice, lines recompressed, is 13.69×. - **The wall at N threads** is the larger of the scanner's time and the workers' time over N (the scanner is one thread; the workers run blocks in parallel), times the sample's own wall over that bound: its overlap and fill taken to grow with the work, which errs long. Read as a fixed cost instead, the same gap gives the third row. - **The machine is this runner,** reading the dump from page cache: no download, no disk, no other work. The output is hashed by the reading thread and discarded. - The uncertainty is the rounds' spread, with the sample ratio's added in quadrature to the part that scales with the output; not the runner's: another CPU model gives other figures. items.title: Throughput–memory frontier
items.text:
In 2001 Seward set the inverse BWT's space–time trade-off for one block: a smaller table (indexF, the byte recovered from the first column) costs more work a step than the merged one (mergedTL, the byte kept beside each link, the layout mibz2 uses). The question here is whether that trade-off still holds when several blocks decode at once and their tables share one L3 cache. A table that is slower for one block might be faster for the machine, if its smaller footprint keeps more blocks resident.

Where it stands: the mechanism is measured, and so is a first shift. On the i9 and the Wikidata corpus, the full decoder with cooperative teams dominates every worker count measured (4 to 20) on both throughput and peak RSS (series 3). Whether it also does at 1 to 3 workers, the low-memory end, is not yet measured.

finding status Shared cache capacity bounds throughput: the knee sits at about 14.4 MB of live tables, 0.7 of the i9's 20 MB L3, at two block sizes measured (workstation journal §9) The table is compressible: about 77% of a full block's rows are in 32-row translation groups measured (ψ census) Sharing a block's table between threads moves the full decoder's throughput–RSS frontier: every worker count from 4 to 20 is dominated by a team configuration measured on one machine and workload, at 4 threads and above (decoder journal, series 3) A compact table can be navigated as fast, built directly from the last column not shown A compact table gives more throughput from less memory than the best 32-bit configuration, on one machine and workload not shown

items.title: Compact navigation tables for the inverse BWT
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

This research began with a simple question:

Can succinct data structures make my bzip2 decoder faster?

The answer so far is that the large table the decoder uses to reconstruct text stores more than it needs to, and much of what it stores follows simple patterns.

This is no longer only theory: a census of the benchmark corpus's actual data shows those patterns.

What follows starts from the beginning and assumes no background in compressed indexes.

items.title: Compact navigation tables for the inverse BWT: early findings
items.text:
Most of the inverse BWT's navigation table follows simple patterns: what a census of real blocks found, and what comes next.

29 October 2026 · 10 min read · Work in progress

items.title: 1. The decoder follows a chain of pointers
items.text:
When bzip2 compresses some text, it performs the Burrows–Wheeler Transform (BWT).

The BWT rearranges the characters in a way that helps compression. But recovering the original text requires following a particular sequence of positions.

Imagine an enormous collection of numbered cards.

Each card tells you which card to visit next.

A miniature pointer chain

  1. Card 03→
  2. Card 15→
  3. Card 20→
  4. Card 36→
  5. Card 41→
  6. Card 52→
  7. Card 64→
Currently at card 01 of 7 visited Follow pointer →Reset

Path: 0 → 3 → 6 → 4 → 1 → 5 → 2

Each card contains the number of the next card. The highlighted card is the current position: follow the pointers from card 0 until every card has been visited.

mibz2's decoder uses a table called the T-vector, which is essentially a much larger, more sophisticated collection of such cards.

For each position, it stores:

  • Where to go next.
  • The character associated with that position.
  • A marker used by mibz2's cooperative traversal algorithm.

At maximum bzip2 block size, this table occupies approximately 3.6 MB.

mibz2's 32-lane implementation already tackles one major cost: instead of following one chain and repeatedly waiting for memory, it follows many independent chains at once.

That's memory-level parallelism (MLP).

So far, so good.

But then we asked a different question.

Why do we need four bytes for every card?

items.title: 2. The cards aren't arbitrary
items.text:
Take these two sequences of destinations:

Two groups of eight pointers

Group A: arbitrary values42718903617122954846Group B: consecutive values427428429430431432433434Group B in one line: base 427, then add the position (+0, +1, … +7)

For Group A, storing eight values individually is reasonable.

But Group B?

You only need to remember:

Start at 427 and add the position within the group.

One starting number replaces eight separate numbers.

The permutation mibz2's inverse BWT decoder follows, called Ψ (psi), isn't a completely arbitrary permutation.

Because of how the BWT is constructed, it consists of increasing sequences of positions.

That means consecutive entries within a particular character group always point to increasing positions.

They won't necessarily be consecutive like Group B—but they're at least sorted.

And that gives us opportunities to compress them.

This is where succinct data structures entered the picture.
path: Compact navigation tables for the inverse BWT

items.title: 3. Succinct structures are about storing the pattern, not the individual facts
items.text:
In ordinary programming, we tend to store arrays of values directly.

A succinct representation asks:

Can I describe the arrangement of these values more economically and reconstruct any particular value when needed?

For example, rather than storing:

1000, 1002, 1005, 1008, 1010

you might store:

base = 1000

and:

offsets = 0, 2, 5, 8, 10

The offsets are much smaller than the absolute values, so they may require fewer bits.

This is called frame-of-reference encoding, or FOR.

Another technique, Elias–Fano, is especially suited to sorted integer sequences. It separates the higher and lower parts of each number and compresses the high parts using the sequence's monotonicity.

Neither is magic; you save memory at the cost of some work to recover an individual value.

And that creates our main tension:

A more compact table is useful only if reconstructing its pointers doesn't make the decoder slower than before.

items.title: 4. What the census found
items.text:
Initially, we had no idea how well these representations would fit real BWT data.

Perhaps the values were increasing but widely scattered, making compression awkward.

So we wrote a census program to inspect them.

It found more structure than the theory alone guarantees.

What our census found in the benchmark corpus

Simple consecutive groups77.6%Rows where a complete group of pointers can potentially be represented by one base plus a simple offset.Fit compact FOR or Elias–Fano99.51%Only 0.49% of rows required exceptions under the proposed 32-value encoding scheme. These two percentages overlap: they aren't two separate populations.

The important observation is that more than three-quarters of the measured rows may be represented using a simple arithmetic rule.

That is much better than we could have assumed from the mathematics alone.

It's the difference between saying:

This encoding should work in principle.

And:

We've examined the actual pointers, and most of them exhibit precisely the structure this encoding is designed to exploit.

It does not yet mean the decoder will be faster. But it establishes that there is something real to exploit.

items.title: 5. Why the CPU's cache lines became central
items.text:
Now we reach the hardware connection.

Modern CPUs don't fetch arbitrary isolated bytes from main memory one at a time. They work with cache lines, commonly 64 bytes.

Imagine a cache line as a little tray of data.

If the next pointer lives in that tray, the processor can fetch the tray and extract what it needs.

The first design asks:

What if we could store 32 pointers in exactly one 64-byte cache line?

The fixed-cache-line proposal

One cache-line record64 bytes01234567891011121314151617181920212223242526272829303132 logical pointers represented inside a single physical record.Average space per pointer2 bytes

mibz2's current representation uses four bytes per pointer.

So the new design could halve the navigation table's storage, before exception overhead.

And crucially, the record can be found immediately from the current row number.

No searching for where the record was stored.

This is very important because mibz2's greatest strength is how quickly it can issue independent memory requests.

A compact representation that introduces multiple dependent searches could destroy that advantage.

The fixed-size record tries to avoid precisely that.

items.title: 6. A second design: a two-tier layout
items.text:
If 77.6% of rows belong to simple consecutive groups, why devote an entire 64-byte record to each of those groups?

Most of the record would contain information we don't actually need.

So we proposed a two-tier layout.

Two-tier Ψ navigation

Current row numberSmall 8-byte directory entryContains format, markers and either a base or payload addressTranslation groupBase + offsetThe answer is already in the directory entryOther groupLoad extra recordDecode FOR / Elias–Fano / exception

It is a compromise.

For the common case, the small directory entry already gives us the next pointer.

For the less common case, we fetch extra information.

Because the directory is tiny compared with the current T-vector, it may fit much more comfortably in cache.

And because we don't allocate a full 64-byte record for the simple groups, the storage could become much smaller.

Our initial calculation suggested something in the neighbourhood of 5.6 bits per row, before additional exceptions and bookkeeping.

That's not a measured final footprint. It's an optimistic model built from the reported distribution.

The attraction is real, but so is the risk: whenever we need the second record, we introduce another memory dependency.

items.title: 7. Why a smaller table could make mibz2 faster
items.text:
Suppose mibz2 is decoding one full-sized bzip2 block.

Its T-vector for that block is 3.6 MB.

But mibz2 can work on multiple blocks concurrently.

With several full-size blocks in flight, their tables compete for space in the CPU's shared cache.

Eight simultaneous full-block tables

0 MB8 MB16 MB24 MB32 MB28.8 MBCurrent32-bit T-vector21.6 MB24-bitdirect links14.5 MB16-bit fixedcache-line recordsabout 5 MBTwo-tierestimate Illustrative table storage for eight full 900 KB blocks. The two-tier estimate (dashed) excludes additional exception and alignment overhead.

Earlier measurements on a 10-core workstation already show evidence of a shared-cache residency threshold.

When the live tables become too large, the processor must fetch more data from slower parts of the memory hierarchy.

Smaller tables would let more of them stay resident in the same cache capacity.

We might see fewer expensive memory misses.

Even if each individual pointer is slightly more expensive to decode, the overall decoder could become faster.

This is the same kind of trade-off Julian Seward studied in 2001.

But mibz2 adds modern multicore concurrency and 32-lane traversal.

The goal is not to have the smallest possible table. It's to make the whole machine finish decoding sooner.

items.title: 8. Open questions
items.text:
There are three substantial unanswered questions.

First, how much does decoding a compressed pointer cost? With the current T-vector, the CPU loads a 32-bit value and extracts the next row. With a compressed record, it may need shifts, masks, a format test and sometimes an additional memory access. Even a small amount of extra work matters when repeated millions of times.

Second, how expensive is construction? The compressed table must be built from the BWT before it can be traversed. A representation that makes traversal faster but takes twice as long to build might lose overall.

Third, does the 77.6% translation property hold broadly? We know it appears in our benchmark corpus. We don't yet know how stable it is across different types of compressed data, and it's not a universal mathematical guarantee.

We have enough evidence to investigate these questions seriously, but not enough to claim a faster decoder.

items.title: 9. What is known and what is not
items.text:
Finding Status Ψ has increasing sequences that can be compressed Mathematically established Actual benchmark data contains abundant consecutive-position groups Measured by our census Fixed 64-byte records can represent the overwhelming majority of measured groups Strongly supported by the census; complete encoding still needs validation A two-tier directory could shrink storage further New design hypothesis Reduced working sets can improve cache residency Supported by mibz2's existing performance measurements Either compressed design will beat the current decoder Unknown

And the most important distinction of all:

We've found evidence that the data is compressible in a form suited to fast navigation. We haven't yet proved that navigating the compressed representation is faster.

These are separate claims.

items.title: 10. The underlying idea
items.text:
The underlying point is that the T-vector—the enormous table of navigation pointers—isn't fundamentally necessary in its current form.

It's a convenient way to store answers to questions.

The BWT already contains the information from which those answers can be derived.

Succinct data structures teach us to exploit that fact.

But our work adds an interesting twist:

Rather than pursuing the absolutely smallest possible encoding, we're looking for a carefully chosen amount of redundancy that allows the CPU to recover answers quickly.

In other words, sometimes storing a little unnecessary information makes the whole algorithm faster.

That's what makes the problem so subtle.

A theoretician might ask:

How close can we get to the minimum number of bits?

A systems programmer might ask:

How few instructions can we execute per pointer?

Our research asks:

How should we arrange the information so that the CPU can follow millions of pointers with as little waiting as possible?

That brings information theory, succinct data structures, cache architecture and instruction scheduling together in one problem.

items.title: What comes next
items.text:
The census shows there is structure to exploit. It says nothing yet about speed, and the next steps are the measurements that will. They run in order, one controlled comparison at a time.

The roadmap, in order

1Single-core fused build (#93)Measured: 1.027×Removing the table fill and scattering straight into the T-vector gained 1.027× on CI, under thepre-registered 1.03 floor. On one core the existing build is already about as fast. Kept as anegative result.2Cooperative fused build (#81)Measured: passedOn the 10-core workstation, the one-pass cooperative build ran 1.31× the two-pass one at 3×3 (20of 20 rounds), and build and walk together 1.10×, past the pre-registered 1.15× bar. Not yet adecoder figure: the checkpoints were given free and the MTF stage untimed.3The cooperative path in the decoderNextBring the cooperative build and walk into the decoder behind an option and measure it end toend, from .bz2 file to checked output, against today's decoder at the same core count.4Audit the F-byte lookup (#79)NextRead the generated code of the existing F-window lookup that recovers each output byte.5Embedded byte vs F recovery (#79)NextOne traversal kernel, lane scheduler and start-marker handling; only how the output byte isrecovered changes. That decides whether a 24-bit table is viable.6Compact Ψ, built directlyLaterExact layouts for the fixed-record and two-tier designs, and the cost of building their recordsstraight from the BWT, never making the 32-bit table at all.7Navigation-cost harnessLaterDirect links, fixed 64-byte records and two-tier descriptors on a matched pointer-chasingworkload, the second dependent load included.8Decoder prototypeIf justifiedConstruction, traversal, exceptions and concurrency together, before any change to theproduction decoder. Each step's prediction and pass and fail thresholds are written down before it runs. Status on 29 October 2026, after the workstation run of #81.

The first of them has now run. Building the table in one pass, rather than copying first and scattering after, made the cooperative build 1.31× faster on the 10-core workstation. That raises the bar for every compact design: each must now beat the fused 32-bit build and its walk, not the old two-pass one.

It also sharpens the question. The most interesting version of a compact table is not one made by compressing a finished T-vector, but one built straight from the BWT, record by record, so the full 32-bit table is never written at all. Writing fewer bytes need not mean doing less work, so that too will be measured before anything is built on it.

Three table designs are kept as candidates. None is built yet, and they will compete on measured construction and navigation cost, not on size alone:

  • 24-bit direct links: the simple reference, a quarter smaller than today's table.
  • Fixed 64-byte records: 32 pointers to a cache line, 16.16 bits a row on the corpus.
  • Two-tier descriptors: 5.70 bits a row on the corpus, but 12–36% of steps need a second, dependent load, and on less regular inputs the design loses its advantage.

This post will be updated as the results come in. The work is tracked on #81 and #79.

items.text:
We've moved from:

"Maybe succinct data structures could save us some memory."

To:

"We have evidence that most of the permutation can be represented by simple rules, and we have several concrete ways of exploiting those rules while protecting the memory-level parallelism that makes mibz2 fast."

We now have a real engineering question to settle: whether those smaller representations can make the CPU finish its work faster.

The working hypothesis, in one line:

A decoder may get faster not by following its pointers more efficiently, but by not storing most of them individually.

Since this was written

The census has since been refined and the designs' sizes counted exactly. On the corpus's 233 full blocks:

  • 77.39% of rows are in groups that are one run, ranging from 63.7% to 88.0% per block;
  • the fixed 64-byte records come to 16.16 bits a row;
  • the two-tier design comes to 5.70 bits a row, where 12–36% of steps need its second lookup.

On other inputs, such as random or already-compressed data, runs are rare. There the two-tier design is larger than the fixed records, while the fixed records still fit at about 16.3 bits a row. The details, sources and the full discussion are in the research journal (docs/journal/2026-10-29-succinct-review.md, #94) and on #79.

items.title: 32 lanes, 8.6 chains
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

This post asks how much parallel work the CPU actually does inside mibz2's inverse-BWT decoder, and whether hardware capacity is lost to the way Rust compiles the loop.

The interesting part is that the suspected problem may not be too little parallelism at all. The figures could instead mean that the CPU already hides memory latency well, but spends too many instructions on each decoded byte.

items.title: 32 lanes, 8.6 chains: where the inverse BWT walk spends its cycles
items.text:
The decoder's 32-lane walk runs 8.6 times faster than one chain. That figure may not mean what it seems: the walk may already hide memory latency, and spend too many instructions on each byte.

31 October 2026 · 7 min read · Open question

items.title: 1. Why does the BWT decoder have 32 lanes?
items.text:
The inverse BWT repeatedly looks up the next position in a table. Simplifying the actual code:

let q = t[row];
row = q >> 8;
output.push(q as u8);

The next lookup depends on the result of the previous one: ri+1 = Ψ(ri).

The CPU cannot know where to look next until the current lookup completes. This is called pointer chasing, and along one chain it is inherently serial.

mibz2's answer is to divide the inverse-BWT traversal into 512 segments and walk up to 32 independent segments at once. Each lane has its own row position, destination and segment state.

Independent traversal chains

in flight togetherLane 0lookup 1lookup 2lookup 3lookup 4lookup 5Lane 1lookup 1lookup 2lookup 3lookup 4lookup 5Lane 2lookup 1lookup 2lookup 3lookup 4lookup 5⋮⋮ 28 more lanes ⋮Lane 31lookup 1lookup 2lookup 3lookup 4lookup 5timeAlong a lane, each lookup waits for the previous one. Across lanes, nothing waits. Four of the 32 lanes. Within a lane, each lookup waits for the one before it; across lanes, the CPU can overlap the lookups.

The source calls this walk room_segments::<32, PF_L1>. The PF_L1 part enables a prefetch hint for the next T-vector entry. The "room" algorithm batches output writes to avoid a buffer-capacity check on every byte, but it still performs one dependent lookup for every decoded byte.

items.title: 2. Where does "8.6 effective chains" come from?
items.text:
Two measured figures:

Measurement Cost One dependent chain 38.55 cycles/byte The 32-lane room walk 4.49 cycles/byte

Their ratio is 38.55 ÷ 4.49 = 8.59.

So the walk achieves about 8.6 times the byte rate of the serial chain, provided the two measurements are comparable. It does not mean that only 8.6 of the 32 lanes are working.

That distinction decides whether the next optimisation should look for more parallelism, or for less work per byte.

items.title: 3. Why 32 lanes might yield only an 8.6× speed-up
items.text:
Imagine a processor that takes 39 cycles to complete a dependent table lookup. If one lookup starts every 4.49 cycles, the average number in progress is about 39 ÷ 4.49 ≈ 8.7.

That is Little's law: concurrency equals request rate multiplied by latency. Computer architecture distinguishes this achieved memory-level parallelism from the number of independent chains a program makes available.

But consider what that means for mibz2. A full round of the walk, one step for each of the 32 lanes, takes 32 × 4.49 ≈ 144 cycles.

One round of the room walk, against one lookup's latency

One round: the walker steps each of its 32 lanes once, one step every 4.49 cycleslane 0lane 0 again32 × 4.49 ≈ 144 cyclesEach step starts a lookup that takes about 38.55 cycles to come backat any moment ≈ 38.55 ÷ 4.49 ≈ 8.6 lookups in progresslane 0’s lookup is back long before its next turn: all 32 lanes keep moving without 32 loads in flight Illustrative, from the two measured figures above. About 8.6 lookups overlap at any moment, yet every lane's lookup returns long before that lane's next turn.

If a lookup takes roughly 39 cycles, the CPU has ample time to finish a lane's lookup before it comes back to that lane in the next round. So all 32 lanes can be making progress without 32 loads ever being in flight at once.

That would place the bottleneck somewhere else.

There is another caveat. The room walk explicitly prefetches future entries, so its actual demand-load latency may be much lower than the 38.55 cycles of the single chain. The two figures also need the same CPU, revision and cache conditions. So 8.6 is best read as an illustrative latency-hiding factor, not a measured count of outstanding memory requests.

items.title: 4. What to look for in the machine code
items.text:
Here is one iteration of the hot loop, simplified:

for lane in lanes.iter_mut() {
    let q = t[lane.row];                   // dependent load
    if q & START != 0 { /* handoff */ }    // branch
    lane.row = q >> 8;                     // next link
    prefetch(t, lane.row);                 // future memory request
    *base[lane_index].add(off) = q as u8;  // output store
}

Several explanations compete:

Suspected limit What it means Register pressure Too few architectural registers to hold all 32 lanes' row and output state, so the generated loop keeps reloading and storing bookkeeping Instruction-window pressure Too many instructions separate successive independent T-vector loads, which limits what the CPU can have in flight Execution throughput Address generation, branches, prefetches and stores use enough execution resources to set a floor in cycles per byte Memory-system saturation The core already overlaps enough lookups, and exposing more chains won't help

A Zen 3 core, for example, has a 256-entry reorder window and a finite number of load and miss-tracking resources: substantial, but not unlimited.

Reading the disassembly, not just the Rust, shows which dependencies LLVM actually creates. One promising possibility is that the CPU spends too much time maintaining lane.row, lane.seg, lane.p and lane.end relative to the useful BWT lookup.

The segment-start branch, by contrast, is rarely taken: about 512 boundaries per 900,000 bytes, or 0.057% of steps. Even a 20-cycle misprediction at every boundary costs only about 0.011 cycles per byte, so boundary mispredictions alone can't explain an opportunity of more than 1 cycle per byte. The throughput of the per-byte branch and bookkeeping could still matter.

items.title: 5. What does "four groups of eight" mean?
items.text:
This is scalar batching, not necessarily SIMD. The idea is to arrange the 32 logical lanes as four groups of eight, so that each group's working state is easier for the compiler to keep in registers.

But there's a trap.

Batching the 32 lanes as four groups of eight

Interleaved groupseach step touches every groupgroup 0group 1group 2group 332 chains exposedbookkeeping per group, overlap keptOne group at a timeseveral rounds of group 0, then group 1, …group 0group 1group 2group 38 chains exposedlatency floor ≥ 38.55 ÷ 8 = 4.82 c/B (today: 4.49) Green lanes have a lookup the CPU can overlap. Batching helps only if every group still has lookups in flight within the processor's instruction window.

If an implementation runs several rounds of group 0 before touching groups 1 to 3, it may expose only eight independent chains to the CPU at once. Under the idealised 38.55-cycle latency, eight chains have a latency floor of 38.55 ÷ 8 = 4.82 cycles per byte, already slower than today's 4.49.

That doesn't prove batching fails: real latency changes with prefetching and caching. But it shows how saving register operations can lose to reduced overlap.

The better transformation reduces lane bookkeeping while still exposing independent loads from all four groups within the processor's instruction window.

items.title: 6. What would count as a breakthrough?
items.text:
The question is which of two fundamentally different paths applies.

Two diagnoses, two different optimisations

Path AInsufficient overlapGenerated code serialises loads thatthe algorithm keeps independent.Fix: remove those dependencies,without spilling lane state.Path B · current hypothesisToo much work per byteOverlap is already sufficient; theinstruction stream sets the pace.Fix: fewer reloads, address and outputsteps per byte, all 32 chains kept. Path B is an inference from the lane-count curve flattening near 24 lanes and from the 32-lane walk already tolerating one chain's latency. It is not yet a verified machine-code finding.

Path A, insufficient overlap: show that the generated code serialises independent loads unnecessarily, then remove those dependencies without giving up register locality or adding costly memory traffic.

Path B, too much work per byte: show that overlap is already sufficient and that the core is limited by its instruction stream, then reduce row-state reloads, address calculations or output bookkeeping while keeping all 32 chains.

The current hypothesis leans towards Path B, given that the measured lane-count curve flattens near 24 lanes, and that the 32-lane scheme already tolerates one chain's latency. That is an inference, not a verified finding.

So the question to settle is:

Are the 32 chains insufficiently exposed, or are they already exposed well enough, while the processor wastes cycles advancing each one?

The two answers call for completely different optimisations, which is why a careful, disassembly-level investigation is worth doing.

A way to save roughly 1.2 cycles per walked byte, on the later decoder baseline of 10.78 cycles per byte, would be worth about 11% of total decoder time, before any gain from the MTF stage. That is why this direction has much greater breakthrough potential than further polishing the MTF selector.

items.title: Block dispatch in mibz2
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

mibz2 has two very different kinds of parallelism:

  1. Across blocks: different CPU cores decompress different bzip2 blocks at the same time.
  2. Within a block: each worker follows 32 independent chains through the inverse BWT's table, to hide memory latency. The previous post is about that one.

This post is about the first kind: how work is handed to the workers, and an apparent delay in that handoff that may or may not be a real bottleneck. Finding out which takes a short tour of mutexes, futexes and the Linux scheduler.

items.title: Block dispatch in mibz2: mutexes, futexes and the scheduler
items.text:
How mibz2's parallel decoder hands blocks to its workers, why some take up to a millisecond to be picked up, and how to tell lock contention from scheduling delay.

1 November 2026 · 12 min read · Investigation in progress

items.title: 1. The journey of a bzip2 block
items.text:
The journey of a bzip2 block through mibz2

Compressed streamA long sequence of bzip2 blocks, read in chunks by the feeder thread (mibz2-read)Scanner · mibz2-scanFinds each block in order, reads its header and Huffman-decodes its symbolsShared job channel · Mutex<Receiver<Job>>Worker 0 · mibz2-0one block at a timeWorker 1 · mibz2-1one block at a timeWorker 2 · mibz2-2one block at a timeWorker 3 · mibz2-3one block at a timeMove-to-front, the inverse BWT, RLE1 and the block's CRCready · a map keyed by block positionEach worker publishes its finished block here, in whatever order it finishesReader · the caller's own threadTakes the blocks in stream order and hands back their bytes Seven threads in all at four workers: the feeder, the scanner, four workers and the caller's thread as the reader. At most a fixed number of blocks (the window, slots) is between the scanner and the reader at any time.

A bzip2 block goes through several stages. In mibz2 they are split between two kinds of thread:

Stage Thread Why there Find the block, read its header, Huffman-decode its symbols the scanner A block's end is only known once its symbols are read, so this part is sequential Move-to-front and its run expansion a worker Independent per block Inverse BWT: build the table, walk it a worker The expensive part, and independent per block RLE1 and the block's CRC a worker Independent per block

This split matters for everything below: a faster inverse BWT can't help if the scanner, or the handoff of jobs to workers, becomes the limit.

All seven threads (the feeder, the scanner, four workers and the reader) share the CPUs the operating system gives them. In the measurements below that is four physical cores, so there are moments when more threads could run than there are cores to run them.

items.title: 2. Two waits in three lines of Rust
items.text:
Here is how a worker gets its next job, from src/parallel.rs:

let job = {
    let rx = jobs.lock().unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner());
    rx.recv()
};

jobs is a Mutex<Receiver<Job>>: one standard-library channel receiver, shared by all the workers behind a mutex. Two different waits can happen here:

  1. Waiting for the mutex. Another worker holds it, so this one can't reach recv().
  2. Waiting for a job. This worker holds the mutex, but the channel is empty, so recv() parks the thread until the scanner sends something.

The second wait happens while the mutex is held: the guard rx lives until the end of the block. That makes possible a situation that is easy to miss in the code:

Four workers, one shared receiver

Worker AAsleep inside recv(): no job yetHolds the receiver mutexWorker BWaiting for the receiver mutexCannot reach recv() at allWorker CDecoding a blockWorker DDecoding another blockThe scanner enqueues two jobsA must wake, return from recv() and drop the lock before B can even start waiting for one The possible receiver convoy. A true multi-consumer queue would let A and B wait for jobs independently. Whether this sequence happens often enough to matter is what the diagnostic measures.

None of this is incorrect. Every job is still taken exactly once, in order. The question is only whether it is slow.

items.title: What a futex is
items.text:
When worker B "waits for the mutex", what actually happens? On Linux, Rust's standard Mutex is a single atomic word, with a futex ("fast userspace mutex") behind it.

How a futex-backed mutex waits

Worker B wants the receiver mutexRust's std Mutex on Linux: one atomic word, and a futex behind itThe lock is freeOne atomic compare-and-swap, entirely in userspace.No system call, no kernel involvement.Fast pathThe lock is heldSpin briefly, then futex(FUTEX_WAIT): the kerneltakes the thread off the CPU until it is woken.Contended pathUnlock: futex(FUTEX_WAKE)The kernel makes one waiter runnable.Runnable is not running: it still needs a CPU. Only the contended path reaches the kernel, which is why kernel traces see futex calls for contention and never for an uncontended lock. The trace marks in mibz2's own code cover both.

A futex is the kernel's way of letting a thread sleep on an address until another thread says "wake up". Most lock operations never need it. The channel's recv() sleeps the same way: it parks the thread on a futex of its own.

items.title: 3. Woken is not running
items.text:
This is the distinction the whole investigation turns on. A thread can be in three states:

State Using a CPU? What it means Running Yes Executing instructions, possibly stalled on memory Runnable No, not yet Ready to execute; waiting for the scheduler to give it a CPU Asleep No Waiting for an event: a futex wake, a job, a lock

A worker's wake-up, in three states

Runnable, not runningReady to execute; waiting for the scheduler to give it a CPUAsleepParked in recv() or on the mutexRunningTakes the lock, receivesJob arrivesWorker wokenWorker runningJob claimed Conceptual timing, not measured values. A futex moves a thread from asleep to runnable; only the scheduler moves it from runnable to running.

So when a job takes a long time to be claimed, there are at least three different explanations, each calling for a different response:

Explanation What would help Mutex ownership: the worker is asleep because another worker owns the receiver A true multi-consumer queue, so idle workers wait independently Scheduling: the worker is runnable, but every CPU is busy with another thread Nothing in the queue, and perhaps nothing at all if those threads are doing useful work Backlog: every worker is busy decoding, so the job simply waits its turn Nothing in the queue: decoding faster

A simple application-level trace can't tell these apart. All three show up as "the job was enqueued at t₀ and claimed at t₁".

items.title: 4. What the traces have shown so far
items.text:
The decoder can record its own timeline: a mark at each step of each thread, with a nanosecond timestamp. On an i9-10900K, decoding a 207 MB slice of Wikidata at four workers, some jobs took nearly a millisecond to be claimed. That looked suspicious, until the delays were sorted by how busy the workers were when the job arrived:

Most slow claims are queueing

Workers decoding when the job arrivedMedian time from enqueue to claim0 of 49% of jobs49.5 µs1 of 417% of jobs48.4 µs2 of 430% of jobs61.6 µs3 of 441% of jobs977 µs4 of 43% of jobs1,221 µs The i9-10900K's ten four-worker traces of the Wikidata corpus. With three or four workers busy, the next job usually waits behind decoding already under way: ordinary queueing, not evidence of lock contention by itself.

Most of the slow claims are backlog. But a smaller set is more interesting: jobs that arrived with three workers decoding, no older job waiting, and one worker free. For those, the free worker's last recorded step tells us where it was:

The free worker's last mark when the job arrived Cases Median time to claim JobRecv: holding the mutex, inside recv() 198 42 µs JobLock: about to take the mutex 149 454 µs

When the free worker is already inside recv(), it claims the job in a median of 42 µs. When it is still trying to take the mutex, it takes ten times as long, and another worker claimed the job first in 89 of the 149 cases.

That gap could be mutex contention. But the kernel's own accounting of each thread's run-queue wait, read between decodes, points elsewhere: in the 120 gaps between decodes that contain such a JobLock case, 78% of the elapsed time was runnable but not running. The workers were awake and eligible to run, but weren't on a CPU. Across all the gaps between decodes, the figure is 34%.

That still doesn't make the delay waste. With seven threads on four cores, a runnable worker may simply be waiting while the scanner or another worker does useful work. The question is what the other CPUs were doing at that moment.

items.title: 5. The reader has its own wait
items.text:
When a worker finishes a block it doesn't write to the output. It publishes the block into a shared ready map keyed by its position, and the reader takes blocks strictly in order.

Blocks finish out of order

#0Still decoding#1Ready#2Ready#3ReadyThe reader cannot hand back block 1 before block 0, though blocks 1–3 are finished.Four slots are held until #0 is done; with a window of eight, the scanner can admit only four more. Finished blocks wait in ready for their turn. The bounded window keeps that wait from turning into unbounded memory.

The scanner is held back by a bounded admission window: at most slots blocks may be between the scanner and the reader (eight at four workers). Before reading the next block, the scanner waits:

while !st.cancelled && st.issued - st.taken >= shared.slots {
    st = shared.cv.wait(st).unwrap_or_else(|e| e.into_inner());
}

That keeps memory bounded when one slow block holds up the reader.

The scanner and the reader share one condition variable, shared.cv, though they wait for different things: the scanner for a free slot, the reader for the next block in order. Workers call notify_all() when they publish a block, and the reader calls it when it takes one. That is correct, but every notification wakes both kinds of waiter, whether or not its own condition changed. Earlier measurements suggested the reader is sometimes late to take a block that is already ready. Whether notification, the lock or scheduling causes that is still open.

items.title: 6. Measuring it without fooling ourselves
items.text:
To separate the three explanations, the next experiment joins two views of the same run:

  • The decoder's own marks, now at every boundary that matters: the attempt to take the receiver mutex, holding it, recv() returning, the guard's release, the decode, the publication, and the reader's waits and wake-ups. Each thread records into a fixed, preallocated buffer, with its operating-system thread id.
  • The kernel's scheduler events, recorded with perf on the allocated CPUs: every wake-up, every switch of a CPU from one thread to another, and every futex wait with its address.

With both, every moment a worker spends not decoding while a job is available can be classified. Was it asleep while another worker owned the receiver? Asleep in the handoff, with the mutex free? Runnable but not running, and if so, what was occupying each CPU? Or publishing, or waiting on the shared lock?

Joining them needs care:

  • Two clocks. The marks use Rust's Instant, and the kernel stamps its events with its own clock. The decoder reads CLOCK_MONOTONIC and immediately makes a recognisable system call, so the gap between the two clocks can be measured from the trace itself. On the preparation machine it is known to within 0.6 µs.
  • The instrument changes what it measures. Each instrumented run is paired with an uninstrumented one. If tracing moves throughput or CPU time by more than 3%, the result is reported as provisional.
  • The decision rules were written down before any data. An isolated multi-consumer queue experiment is justified only if receiver-specific obstruction is at least 5% of the workers' total time, in at least 80% of runs. Runnable time near the mutex is reported beside that, but never counted in it, because it may be ordinary competition for the cores.

items.title: When the instrument lies
items.text:
The preparation runs turned up a lesson worth sharing. A review of the analysis asked a pointed question: could lost kernel events pass unnoticed? Checking it showed they could. perf script prints nothing about events it dropped unless asked with --show-lost-events. Events whose thread perf couldn't resolve were printed in a form the parser skipped.

The surprise came from the kernel itself. On the virtual machine used for preparation, the kernel emitted every switch into idle on three of its four CPUs, but never a switch out of idle. perf's raw dump and ftrace showed the same, so it isn't perf or the parser.

When the instrument lies

What happenedasleeprunnablerunningasleepWhat the trace saidasleeprunnable … still “runnable”asleepAt the green line, the switch from idle into the worker was never emitted (CPUs 1–3).The worker later switched out while “runnable”: the contradiction that gave it away. On the preparation VM, the kernel recorded switches into idle on three of its four CPUs but never the switches out. Running time read as waiting. The analysis now marks such intervals unknown, and refuses a run whose idle switches don't pair.

The effect was subtle and pointed in a dangerous direction. A worker switched in from idle appeared to be woken but never running, so its running time was classified as waiting for a CPU, which is exactly the "scheduling" explanation. In one run, 19 ms of the 77 ms counted as runnable was this artifact.

Now, the analysis:

  • treats any interval the scheduler stream contradicts as unknown;
  • requires every CPU's switches into and out of idle to pair up;
  • runs a short probe before any capture, and refuses to start on a kernel that fails it.

A wrong answer delivered confidently would have been worse than no answer.

items.title: 7. Two problems, one CPU
items.text:
Even with perfect dispatch, four workers each decode less efficiently than one. On the i9, four workers spend about 30% more cycles per decoded byte than one worker, while executing almost the same instructions (1.3% more). The extra cycles go to stalls on memory: each worker's inverse-BWT table competes for the same 20 MB last-level cache, alongside the input, output and intermediate buffers.

Two problems, one CPU

Dispatch efficiencyKeep the workers supplied with jobs andwaste no time waiting.Futexes, the mutex, the scheduler, the channel, notificationsDecoding efficiencySpend fewer cycles and less memorybandwidth on each block.BWT tables, prefetch, cache residency, buffers Better dispatch uses the cores more fully; better decoding makes each core's work cheaper.

These interact. Better dispatch keeps more inverse-BWT walks running at once, which raises the competition for cache and claws back part of its own gain. That is why every experiment is judged on the whole decoder's throughput and CPU-seconds per GB, never on one stage in isolation.

items.title: 8. What happens next
items.text:
The measurement comes next. It ends in one of two places:

  • If receiver ownership really does keep free workers from available jobs, at least 5% of their time in at least 80% of runs, a multi-consumer queue becomes a justified, isolated experiment.
  • If the receiver is usually free and the delay is scheduling or backlog, that hypothesis is retired, and the effort goes to the larger problem: the inverse BWT's memory behaviour.

This post is a snapshot of an investigation in progress, and its figures come from the traces available so far. A few lines of synchronisation code can decide how well a 32-lane, latency-hiding decoder uses a whole multicore CPU. Whether they do here is a question for the evidence.

Sources:

  • the worker, scanner and reader loops: src/parallel.rs;
  • the i9 traces and the cycle accounting: the resource attribution's analysis;
  • the diagnostic's registered protocol: 2026-11-01-dispatch-causality-protocol.md;
  • the trace-completeness checks: amendment 1.

items.title: Inverse-BWT memory interference
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

A bzip2 file is a series of independent blocks, so four CPU cores can decode four blocks at once, each with its own data, its own working memory and its own instructions. That's what mibz2 does, and a file finishes much sooner on four cores than on one.

You'd expect the total work to stay about the same, just spread across more cores. It doesn't. With four workers instead of one, mibz2 spends about 32% more CPU time, added up over all the cores, for every gigabyte it decodes.

Little of the extra time goes on handing work between threads. Most of it is inside the decoding itself, where the decoder runs almost the same instructions per byte as before (1.3% more) but needs about 30% more processor cycles to get through them. The same instructions are running slower.

Memory is the obvious suspect. The most expensive step in decoding a block is undoing the Burrows–Wheeler transform, which means following a long chain of links through a table of about 3.6 MB. A core working alone can keep much of that table close at hand in the processor's caches. With four cores at work, four such tables, along with the buffers each worker uses to build and assemble its output, all have to share the processor's last-level cache and the hardware that serves its memory requests.

The suspected problem

One workerCore 1following its table's linksTable AShared cache:room to spareOne table in the shared cacheFour workersCore1ACore2BCore3CCore4DFour tables competing for the same cache A sketch, not a measurement of what's in the cache. Each core has its own table, but all four share the last-level cache and the path to main memory.

If that's what's happening, one worker's memory accesses push out data that another worker was about to use, so its next lookup has to fetch it from further away. Or the shared cache is simply busier, so every request takes longer to answer. Either way, the core spends more of its cycles waiting for data. That's what we mean by memory interference: workers whose logic is independent, competing for the same hardware.

The measurements point that way, but they don't settle it. This post is about two experiments proposed to find out more. One changes how the decoder reuses its memory, and measures whether the extra cost shrinks. The other keeps one decoder fixed and varies what the other cores do with memory, to see which kinds of competition reproduce the slowdown. We're starting with the first, and the rest of the post explains why.

items.title: Investigating inverse-BWT memory interference in mibz2
items.text:
Four workers finish decompression sooner, but together spend 32% more processor time per byte. We're testing whether competition for shared memory is responsible.

1 November 2026 · 14 min read · Research in progress

items.title: 1. What a worker does with each block
items.text:
Each block goes through five steps. Two of the worker's memory buffers, ll and rle, come up throughout the rest of the post.

From compressed symbols to decoded bytes

1. ll — the transformed bytesMTF decoding recovers the bytes as the Burrows–Wheeler transform left them: rearranged2. T-vector — the navigation tableBuilt by reading ll once. Each entry says where to go next, and which byte to write3. Traverse and assemble32 independent chains each rebuild a stretch of the block; the pieces are then copied together in order4. rle — the reconstructed bytesBack in the original order, but runs of a repeated byte are still stored in a short form5. RLE1 — the final expansionExpands those runs into the decompressed output, and checks the block's checksum What a worker does with each block. The worker keeps ll and rle from block to block and refills them each time.
  1. ll holds the transformed bytes. bzip2 compressed the block after rearranging its bytes with the Burrows–Wheeler transform (BWT), and the move-to-front (MTF) decoding stage recovers those rearranged bytes into ll. They are the right bytes in the wrong order: the last column of the transform's sorted table.
  2. The T-vector is built from ll. Building this table reads each byte of ll once. Each entry says which row comes next and which byte to write, so following the links from the right starting point spells out the block in its original order. An earlier post explains the table in more detail.
  3. The traversal follows the links, and assembly joins the pieces. Each lookup depends on the one before, so a single chain of lookups spends most of its time waiting for memory. mibz2 runs 32 chains at once, each rebuilding its own stretch of the block, and switches between them while one waits (the 32 lanes post covers how). The finished stretches are then copied, in order, into one buffer.
  4. That buffer is rle. The block is back in its original order, with one encoding left: before applying the transform, bzip2 had shortened every run of four or more identical bytes into a few bytes and a count.
  5. RLE1 expands those runs into the decoded output, and checks the block's checksum (CRC).

ll and rle aren't registers, and they aren't algorithms. They are two areas of memory holding the same block at different stages: ll before the BWT is undone, rle after it but before the runs are expanded. In the code they are two fields of each worker's scratch space:

ll: Vec<u8>,   // The BWT's last column, written by MTF
rle: Vec<u8>,  // The assembled sequence, before RLE1 expands its runs

items.title: 2. Where the extra time goes
items.text:
We measure efficiency in CPU-seconds per gigabyte of decoded output (CPU-s/GB): the processor time of all the workers added together, per GB produced. Four workers decode a file in much less time than one, but on this measure they cost more.

The cost of decoding on four cores
