Measured on four physical cores. Left: the whole decoder. Right: the traversal and assembly step, on 197 matched full-sized blocks. Both measure CPU time, not elapsed time.

The whole decoder goes from 2.707 to 3.579 CPU-s/GB. Timing each step of each block separately shows where the increase lands:

Step One worker, ns per row Four workers, ns per row Increase MTF decoding 0.456 0.487 1.07× T-vector construction 0.497 0.571 1.15× Traversal and assembly 1.234 1.806 1.46× RLE1 and CRC 0.134 0.180 1.35×

Traversal and assembly take about 79% of the added time across these four steps. Over the whole file, short blocks included, they add about 0.61 CPU-s/GB.

The timing so far can't split that step in two. It covers both the link-following and the copying of the finished pieces into rle, so we don't yet know how much of the 1.46× belongs to each.

The traces also show a pattern. A block's traversal took a median 1.29× its one-worker time when no other worker was traversing at the same moment, and 1.66× when all three others were. That fits the memory story, but it doesn't prove it: a slower traversal also overlaps more of the others' traversals simply by lasting longer.

items.title: 3. Why the counters don't settle it
items.text:
The processor's performance counters narrow things down without picking a culprit.

Per decoded byte, the number of data requests that miss each core's private caches barely changes between one and four workers. Each request seems to take longer, though: by an approximate measure, it stays outstanding for about 58 processor cycles rather than 39. Traffic to main memory (DRAM) also rises sharply, especially writes.

Those clues fit several explanations:

  • The tables crowd each other out. Each worker's table pushes the others' entries out of the last-level cache (the L3, shared by all the cores), so more lookups have to go to DRAM.
  • The shared cache is congested. The lookups still find their data in the L3, but they queue for longer because four cores are asking at once.
  • The writes get in the way. To write to memory, a core first takes exclusive ownership of the cache line, and the changed line must later be written back. Writes can also push out useful data and tie up the hardware that loads and prefetches need.

These feed into each other. A little more eviction makes prefetches arrive later, later requests hold hardware resources for longer, and that slows the requests behind them. The counters can't tell us which one starts the chain.

The request-duration figure is a good example. It counts the prefetches the traversal issues in advance alongside the lookups it actually waits for, so it shows that memory behaviour changed without telling us how long any single lookup waited. And the extra DRAM writes could be a symptom rather than a cause: the same crowding that slows the traversal would produce them too. The research record has the counters in full.

So there are two ways forward: change how the decoder uses memory and see what happens, or recreate the competition under controlled conditions and see what it does. Astra and Claude each proposed one.

items.title: 4. Astra's proposal: write the output into ll
items.text:
Our research register is a list of about 165 ideas for speeding up the decoder, gathered from the project's journals, branches, issues and pull requests, each with its status and what would test it. Entry P87, "walk output in L's freed buffer", had been recorded there but never tried. Astra's experiment is a careful test of it.

The idea rests on when each buffer's contents stop mattering. Once the T-vector is built, nothing reads the bytes in ll again for that block: the traversal reads only the table. The bytes are dead, but the memory holding them, about 0.9 MB for a full block, is still allocated, and it sits idle until the next block's MTF output fills it.

P87 writes the assembled bytes into that idle memory instead of into rle. The bytes written are identical, and so is the copy that writes them. What changes is which memory the copy lands in.

The proposed P87 comparison

A · Current decoderAssembled bytes go to separate storagell: BWT last-column bytesWritten by MTF · about 0.9 MBT-vector construction reads llThe last use of ll's contentsTraversal: temporary segments32 lanes, each a stretch of the blockAssemble into separate rleIts own storage, written every blockRLE1 expands rle into the final outputB · P87Assembled bytes reuse ll's storagell: BWT last-column bytesWritten by MTF · about 0.9 MBT-vector construction reads llNow ll's contents are no longer neededTraversal: temporary segmentsThe same lanes, the same segmentsAssemble into reusable llThe same bytes, over the dead contentsRLE1 expands ll into the final outputThe assembled bytes are identical in both arms. Only the storage they are written into changes. Both arms build and traverse the same table, produce the same pieces and copy them the same way, so the assembled bytes are identical. Only the memory receiving them differs.

items.title: Why it could help
items.text:
Writing into ll means the worker touches about 0.9 MB less distinct memory per block, and so needs fewer separate cache lines in a writable state. That could mean less of the crowding, fewer ownership requests and fewer write-backs to main memory. Any saving would matter most when another worker is following its own table at the same time.

There's a subtlety in the timing. Assembly happens after the traversal it follows, so changing where the assembly writes can't speed up that same traversal. If the traversal gets cheaper under P87, the saving must come indirectly: from less competition with the other workers, from a different cache state carried into the next block, or from the steps overlapping differently. A cheaper traversal would therefore tell us more than a cheaper assembly.

items.title: Why it might not
items.text:
Both buffers are already reused from block to block. ll was written by MTF and read by the table build shortly before; rle was last read by RLE1 during the previous block. By the time assembly starts, the traversal may have pushed most of either one out of the cache, in which case reusing ll saves nothing.

The experiment measures whether the difference matters rather than assuming it does. To keep the comparison fair, both versions allocate both buffers at full size and touch their memory once in advance. Otherwise a gain could come from simply allocating less, or from the operating system mapping fewer fresh pages. Whether a production version could drop rle altogether, and save the memory, would be a separate question.

items.title: 5. Claude's proposal: vary what the neighbours do
items.text:
Claude's proposal comes at the problem from the other side. Instead of changing the decoder, it measures one decoding worker while controlling what the other three cores do.

The measured worker decodes as usual, building and traversing its tables, with counters around each step. The three neighbouring cores run one chosen kind of workload at a time.

One measured worker, three controlled neighbours

Four physical cores on the same processorCORE 1Target walkerSame decoding workMeasured every armCORE 2NeighbourControlled workloadChanges between armsCORE 3NeighbourControlled workloadChanges between armsCORE 4NeighbourControlled workloadChanges between armsShared last-level cacheCapacity, line replacement, requests and shared-cache contentionMemory controller and DRAM The measured worker is held fixed while the three neighbours run controlled workloads. The diagram shows what the cores share; it doesn't imply that each shared resource can be varied on its own.

Each workload stresses a different part of the memory system:

Neighbour workload What it tests Real decoding work Whether the setup reproduces the real slowdown at all Only traversal, or only table building Whether traversal suffers more from other traversals or from table builds Read-only data of several sizes Whether a bigger footprint in the shared cache makes traversal steadily slower Heavy writers Whether writes and write-backs are especially damaging Many L3 requests from a small footprint Whether request traffic alone, without much cache space, reproduces the slowdown Streaming to and from DRAM Whether main-memory traffic reproduces it

The results could separate the explanations from section 3. If traversal slows steadily as the neighbours' read-only data grows, even though they make few requests, cache capacity looks like the problem. If a small workload making many L3 requests slows it just as much, while large but rarely touched data does little, congestion in the shared cache looks more likely. Neighbours that only traverse, or only build, would also show whether the pattern from section 2, slower traversals when more traversals overlap, holds up under control.

items.title: The catch
items.text:
These workloads don't isolate one hardware resource each. A workload that holds data in the cache has to keep touching it, which makes requests of its own. A heavy writer changes the ownership traffic as well as the write-backs. A DRAM stream can match the decoder's average bandwidth with a quite different mix of reads, writes and bursts. So the experiment would measure how sensitive a traversal is to each kind of neighbour, rather than assign the real slowdown, fraction by fraction, to particular hardware.

It also depends on the setup behaving like the real decoder in the first place. Four independent decoding loops lack the real decoder's scanner, its buffer reuse and its mix of overlapping traversals. Claude proposed requiring real decoding neighbours to reproduce at least 70% of the real slowdown before going further. That's a sensible gate, but failing it would only show that the setup wasn't realistic enough. It wouldn't show that the real decoder is free of interference. Making the setup realistic enough is a project in itself.

items.title: 6. Why P87 comes first
items.text:
P87: reuse ll Controlled neighbours Changes Which memory the assembly writes into What the other cores do with memory Measures The whole decoder's efficiency One fixed traversal's cost Strength Directly tests a change we could ship Can identify a broader cause Limitation Tests one change only Results depend on how realistic the setup is If it succeeds Validate the change for production Design a change aimed at the resource it identifies

P87 doesn't come first because it has more to gain. The neighbour experiment may well point to a bigger opportunity, in how the tables sit in the cache or how requests compete for it. P87 comes first because it asks a smaller question whose answer changes what we do next. If it works, we have an improvement that keeps the current four-byte table and the 32-chain traversal. If it doesn't, we can drop this idea without first having to explain the whole memory system.

items.title: What would count as success
items.text:
Astra proposed measuring both versions, the current one (A) and the one that reuses ll (B), at one worker and at four. Write \(C_{X,w}\) for the CPU-seconds per GB of version \(X\) with \(w\) workers. The saving that appears only under concurrency is then

\[ D = (C_{A,4} - C_{B,4}) - (C_{A,1} - C_{B,1}) \]

which takes the four-worker saving and subtracts whatever saving B already gives a single worker. Astra suggested 0.10 CPU-s/GB as the size that would count as material.

\(D\) answers one question, and a second needs its own test:

MechanismDoes buffer reuse materially reduce theadditional CPU cost associated withconcurrency?Measured by the proposed difference-in-differencesstatistic and its uncertainty.EngineeringIs the actual four-worker decoder fasterand more CPU-efficient, withoutcompromising correctness or memoryrequirements?Measured at the full-decoder boundary.

The two can disagree. A change could make both versions slower while shrinking the gap between them, giving a positive \(D\) with a slower four-worker decoder. And reuse might make assembly or RLE1 cheaper by the same amount at one and four workers: a worthwhile small optimisation, with \(D\) near zero and nothing learned about concurrency.

To tell these cases apart, the experiment times table building, traversal, assembly and RLE1 separately. It also keeps the table building and traversal code identical in both versions, gives both the same memory, and leaves the scheduling of workers alone, so that the comparison is about where the output goes and nothing else.

The research register's original entry for P87 set a different bar, for six to ten workers. That remains a separate question from this four-core experiment.

items.title: 7. Where things stand
items.text:
Neither experiment has shown a speedup yet. P87 is the one we're running first, and the neighbour experiment remains a broader follow-up. What we'd learn depends on the result:

P87 result What it would tell us What we'd do next Faster and cheaper at four workers, with a material \(D\) Where the output goes contributes to the four-worker cost Validate the change, and look at the lifetimes of other buffers Cheaper assembly or RLE1, but \(D\) near zero Reuse helps locally without explaining the traversal slowdown Treat it as a small optimisation Fewer writes to main memory, but the same traversal cost These particular writes weren't what slowed the traversal Stop treating them as a likely cause No meaningful change This kind of reuse doesn't help under these conditions Go back to the neighbour experiment, with a realistic setup The measurement itself proves unreliable Nothing yet Fix the experiment before reading anything into it

Even a material result of 0.10 CPU-s/GB would recover only about 2.8% of the four-worker decoder's CPU cost. That's worth having, but well short of the 1.5–2× gain in throughput we're ultimately after. Getting there will probably take a deeper change to how the table is laid out in memory, how far ahead it's prefetched, or how lookups are served, and the earlier work shows how carefully that has to be done: a smaller table saves cache space for nothing if recovering each link from it becomes too slow. For now the fast four-byte table stays, and P87 leaves it untouched.

The two proposals ask different things. Changing the decoder asks whether one decision about where data lives makes it more efficient. Changing the neighbours asks what kinds of competition make an unchanged traversal more expensive. Both are sound ways to study a performance problem; they just produce different kinds of evidence. We're starting with the direct change because it's smaller, easier to interpret and bears directly on the decoder people use. If it fails, that's a better reason to invest in the broader experiment.

So the question for now is narrower than "why is four-worker decoding expensive?": can writing the output into memory the worker has finished with make concurrent decoding cheaper, without touching the traversal itself?

items.title: MLP: measurement notes
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

These notes accompany the main post. Where the post already explains something fully, they link back to it rather than repeat it. They examine the screenshots reproduced in the post, the historical benchmark behind Daniel Lemire's June 2022 article, primary architecture literature, vendor counter documentation, and the source and archived experiments in lmmx/mibz2. Repository inspection is pinned to the revisions in the source register; sources were inspected on 2 November 2026. Performance results are attributed to their original experiments; no new native benchmark of mibz2 was run for these notes. Numbers in square brackets refer to the register.

items.title: Memory-level parallelism: measurement notes and source record
items.text:
The methodology behind Memory-level parallelism in mibz2: the 2022 benchmark in detail, throughput models, counter definitions and their populations, a measurement programme for mibz2, and the full source register.

2 November 2026 · 16 min read · Source register

items.title: 1. The historical benchmark in detail
items.text: The linked repository is lemire/testingmlp. Its last published revision before the article is 23569032cd784366247c0381e4d532c9a82f3263, from January 2021. That establishes the public implementation available at the time; it doesn't prove the author's exact local checkout or command line. Reading today's changed benchmark as if it were the 2022 implementation would be unsafe. A later post by the same author, [29], uses the evolved benchmark, and its settings shouldn't be conflated with the 2022 test.

items.title: Construction
items.text:
The historical default is an array of 33,554,432 uint64_t entries, 256 MiB. A second array of the same size supports setup, outside the timed traversal. Sattolo's algorithm builds a random permutation that is one long cycle, and the lanes' starting positions are spaced along it. The test uses array-index links and several traversal states, not separately allocated list nodes [2].

The generator emits a distinct function for each lane count, with one local state variable per lane. The inner loop does one dependent lookup for each lane, then repeats. Total useful accesses are approximately fixed at \(H(K) = K \lfloor H/K \rfloor\), so adding lanes changes the schedule of roughly the same accesses rather than multiplying the work. Loop control is amortised over more accesses, and register allocation can change [3].

The timing takes the fastest of five wall-clock trials, and the traversal is kept observable through its returned result. The code collects no retired instructions, actual CPU cycles, request occupancy, cache-source information, page-walk counters or memory-controller traffic [2].

items.title: The bandwidth figure
items.text:
The program computes an implied bandwidth: completed logical accesses times 64 bytes, divided by time. Each architectural load reads eight bytes, so the calculation assumes one cache-line transfer per logical access; it doesn't measure DRAM traffic. The source divides by powers of 1024 while printing MB/s, a small ambiguity in the unit label [2].

Actual traffic differs with cache hits, several entries sharing a line, merged requests, hardware prefetches, page-table reads and other memory activity. Eight 64-bit entries fit in one 64-byte line, so a large random array doesn't guarantee a DRAM transaction for every load. And with several lanes, the ns/hit column is elapsed time divided by aggregate accesses: the reciprocal of throughput, not the service latency of one request.

items.title: What a fair review asks
items.text: The design deliberately makes long-latency dependent loads dominant and uses independent chains to expose overlap. That's a sensible microbenchmark. A stricter review would also ask how much work the compiler adds, where requests are served, whether translation limits the result, how stable the curve is, and how loaded latency changes as lanes are added. The appropriate conclusion is neither that the method is invalid nor that other measurements are unnecessary: it's a useful characterisation with a well-defined workload and limits to its interpretation.

items.title: 2. Saturation, translation and read size
items.text:
The historical code reports a possible number of parallel paths when another lane improves time by less than one percent. A noisy point, a spill threshold or a different resource limit can produce such a knee, so a plateau is an observation that needs interpreting [2]. The main post lists the four quantities often called MLP, which need not be equal: a program may have 32 active lanes and eight outstanding requests on average; a ten-entry resource may contribute to a system that supports a different count at another boundary; and demand loads, hardware prefetches and page walks may occupy overlapping but different resources.

Travis Downs, a collaborator on the benchmark, explains in the 2019 discussion that the core, the uncore, the memory controller and DRAM all affect the observed overlap. Taking the smallest queue capacity is insufficient because a request holds each resource for a different time. The same discussion shows page-size changes materially moving the saturation point [10].

items.title: Translation
items.text:
A 256 MiB region spans 65,536 pages at 4 KiB or 128 at 2 MiB. Those counts are arithmetic; the performance that follows depends on the TLBs and page walkers. A TLB miss may need memory accesses of its own before the data access can go ahead.

The historical README warns about this and recommends transparent huge pages. The source requests MADV_HUGEPAGE, while the article says the tests used small pages. These aren't in conflict: a request for huge pages doesn't establish the pages obtained, Linux can fall back to ordinary pages, and the effective backing has to be checked [4, 30].

For an application comparison, default page behaviour can legitimately be part of the system being compared. To isolate a core's data-miss machinery, translation has to be controlled or measured separately. Both are useful experiments; they answer different questions.

items.title: Read size
items.text:
The exchange's question about how large each read is matters because there are several granularities: the operand size, the cache-line fill, the useful payload consumed, and the page used for translation. A four-byte lookup can need a 64-byte fill, two adjacent four-byte values may share that line, and an access crossing a line boundary may need two. Widening an operand from four to eight bytes doesn't automatically double the memory cost, while growing a node from one line to two can matter a great deal.

The right bandwidth denominator depends on the question. Useful decoded bytes describe the application's productivity; transferred cache lines describe a memory interface; retired loads describe instructions. None substitutes for the others.

items.title: A lower-bound envelope
items.text:
With \(K\) independent chains, recurrence latency \(L\), core execution work per step \(u\), sustainable issue or execution rate \(P\), bytes transferred per step \(b\) and sustainable bandwidth \(B\), an optimistic envelope is

\[ \text{cycles per useful step} \ge \max\left(\frac{L}{K},\ \frac{u}{P},\ \frac{b}{B}\right) \]

with \(L\) in cycles, \(P\) in operations per cycle and \(B\) in bytes per cycle. Separate port limits may matter more than a single aggregate \(P\). It's a reasoning aid, not a calibrated simulator: it leaves out branch recovery, burstiness, queueing and imperfect scheduling.

For a specific resource \(j\), if a useful step needs \(m_j\) requests that each hold the resource for \(W_j\) seconds, and it has \(Q_j\) entries, then

\[ \text{useful steps per second} \le \frac{Q_j}{m_j W_j} \]

That is why taking \(\min(Q_j)\) across unrelated queues is wrong: their occupancy times and request populations differ.

items.title: The bottleneck moves
items.text:
With one chain, \(L/K\) may dominate, and removing independent bookkeeping can do little because the core is waiting for the next address. More chains lower that floor until something else dominates. The main post lists the distinct ways fewer instructions can then help.

More lanes can also make things worse. Lane state may spill to memory, code may grow, output streams may take cache space and write buffers, scheduling can get more expensive, and more concurrency may raise memory queueing and so \(L\) itself. AMAC and Cimple arrange independent memory-bound tasks within one thread and confront exactly these scheduling costs and window limits. Their value here is the mechanism and the experimental framing, not their headline speedups or optimal group sizes [6, 7].

items.title: Little's law needs a boundary and a population
items.text:
For a stable, consistently measured request population:

average outstanding requests = completed requests per second × average seconds per request

If each counted request transfers one line of \(S\) bytes, the line bandwidth is about outstanding × \(S\) ÷ latency. But an application load, a fill-buffer allocation and an offcore transaction needn't correspond one to one.

Time-weighted occupancy needs no CPU-specific assumption. Count the outstanding requests on every cycle and add the counts: a request present for 50 cycles contributes 50. Dividing the sum by total cycles gives average occupancy; dividing it by the number of matching requests gives average residence time, with the boundaries handled appropriately. The main post's figure works one small trace through all three ratios.

Substituting unloaded serial latency for loaded multi-chain latency is only an approximation: queueing, the source of the line and prefetching can all change latency. A higher outstanding count can mean slower service rather than more useful progress, so occupancy should be read together with throughput and residence time.

items.title: 4. Counter definitions and their populations
items.text: The main post covers the three denominators, the conditional L1 metric, the offcore ratio and FB_HIT. These notes add the definitions and the cases that need most care.

items.title: The L1 demand-associated metric
items.text:
Intel defines an MLP metric as L1D_PEND_MISS.PENDING divided by L1D_PEND_MISS.PENDING_CYCLES. Its event definition concerns demand-associated fill buffers. A fill a prefetch started may begin to count once a demand access joins it, and page-walk reads and split accesses complicate the correspondence with source-level loads. It isn't a direct count of independent BWT chains or of DRAM requests [11, 12].

When comparing workers, sum the numerators and denominators before forming a weighted aggregate. That gives a cycle-weighted average per logical processor, not the total number of requests outstanding at once across the machine. An unweighted average of per-thread ratios can hide the fact that some threads or phases account for much more of the time.

items.title: The offcore ratio
items.text: For the relevant Intel event family, OFFCORE_REQUESTS_OUTSTANDING.ALL_DATA_RD integrates outstanding data reads from an L2 miss to completion at the superqueue boundary. Divided by OFFCORE_REQUESTS.ALL_DATA_RD, it gives cycles per request. The population mixes demand reads, prefetches and relevant page-walk reads, and can include requests served by the LLC, so it isn't automatically DRAM latency [11].

items.title: Prefetch and demand-only counts
items.text: A line can arrive before its demand use, or a demand access can join a fill already in flight. A retired demand-load classification describes that load's encounter with the hierarchy, not necessarily the line's full history or where it ultimately came from. MEM_LOAD_RETIRED.FB_HIT says a load merged into a still-pending fill for the same line; the initiating request may have been demand or prefetch, so it doesn't show that the corresponding share of useful work was supplied by prefetch [11].

items.title: Two withdrawn readings
items.text: The corrected mibz2 memory proposal withdraws an earlier estimate that about 98% of walk traffic was prefetch, because retired demand loads reaching L3 and all offcore reads are different populations. It also withdraws reading an inferred count near six as measured, constant walk MLP: the assumed request rate, a mixed process-wide latency proxy and the stage time partly constructed the apparent agreement [25]. Those corrections stand.

items.title: Counter values need causal context
items.text:
More outstanding requests might mean more useful parallel work, or slower service. More DRAM writes might cause contention, or result from evicting dirty data. Fewer retired demand misses might reflect effective prefetching while total traffic grows. A high cache-hit fraction may describe a small, unrepresentative subset of all requests.

Events can also overlap or nest: adding several stall counts is invalid when one cycle belongs to more than one event. Sampling has different semantics from counting, and a sampled instruction address may not identify every contributing cause. A coherent set of counters is evidence for distinguishing hypotheses, not a self-interpreting explanation.

items.title: 5. A measurement programme for mibz2
items.text: The aim is to resolve the remaining ambiguity without repeating experiments the repository has already closed. There are two tracks: a synthetic characterisation to understand a machine, and a production-shaped stage investigation to understand this decoder. The main post gives the measurement sheet and the predictions; these notes add how each track would be run.

items.title: Track A: the machine and the method
items.text:
Compare a single chain, an unrolled version of that same chain, and several interleaved independent chains, holding useful accesses fixed. That separates amortised loop control from inter-chain overlap more cleanly than comparing one chain only with many.

Sweep the active working set through the cache levels and beyond the LLC, and say whether total footprint or footprint per chain is held fixed. Vary node spacing independently of payload size. Compare verified page mappings, not just allocation requests. Establish single-core behaviour before adding physical cores.

Inspect the generated loop at each important lane count, recording spills, branches, instruction size and memory-operation counts. Keep the executable, compiler flags, the input permutation or its hash, affinity, page backing and raw timings. These controls make a knee easier to interpret without pretending to isolate one hardware structure perfectly.

items.title: Track B: the decoder's limiting work
items.text: Use the production sequence of blocks and buffer lifetimes. A prebuilt table traversed repeatedly can be much warmer than one met during decoding; keep cold and warm microbenchmarks if useful, label the conditions, and use the production workload for the shipping decision. Separate table construction, traversal, segment assembly and the later RLE and CRC work, and keep the whole-decoder benchmark, because removing a copy, changing a buffer or growing the code can affect another phase or the other workers. Keep lane count, segment count, prefetch policy and worker count as separate axes.

items.title: Measurement mechanics
items.text:
Small Linux perf event groups can collect matching counters together. For per-thread phase measurements, bracket a substantial block or batch, use consistent filters, keep the enabled and running times, and reject unscheduled groups. Subtract the time metadata as well as the counts when taking interval deltas: resetting counts doesn't reset all the time accounting. Measure the cost of an empty bracket, and keep the original uninstrumented timing [17, 18].

Prefer a few purpose-built groups to one oversized collection that multiplexes heavily. A scaled count assumes the scheduled intervals represent the whole interval, which becomes fragile for short or changing phases. Weigh any gain in precision against the instrumentation's cost and its effect on code layout.

The current sweep covers several lane counts, prefetch hints, and room against flagged walkers; it keeps decode order and has an optional separate PMU pass. Its byte denominator is BWT rows. The phases example reports per final decoded byte, and its c/B column is a nominal-clock conversion [26, 27]. Those distinctions should be recorded beside every result.

items.title: 6. Tools: further notes
items.text:
The main post covers what each tool can establish. Three further points:

  • Static intuition from the source is especially unreliable for a compiler-managed array of lane state. A high-level refactor may produce identical machine code, or a small change may alter register allocation across the loop. Archive the binary that produced each timed result.
  • An LLVM-MCA prediction that disagrees with measured time tells you about missing assumptions in the model; it doesn't show that the measurement must be wrong [15].
  • Cross-ISA IPC is unsuitable as a standalone score: x86 and AArch64 can express the same useful computation in different instruction sequences. Compare useful work per unit time, then use each ISA's own counters to explain the result [13, 14].

Top-down categories narrow a problem; they don't replace studying the useful work and the intervention. A lower-level metric may overlap another or rest on an approximation, and a high retiring fraction can still include avoidable work [31].

items.title: Prefetch lead time is coupled to everything else
items.text:
The walk prefetches one link ahead, but the time before demand returns to a lane depends on the lane count and on the time spent advancing the other lanes. Removing bookkeeping can shorten that interval, so an optimisation may consume a prefetched line sooner and expose more of its latency, even while cutting instructions. That is a hypothesis drawn from the schedule, not a claim that it caused the archived unrolling result; testing it needs timing and request-population evidence. It is also why lane count and instruction cost shouldn't be tuned independently.

A second unknown pointer hop usually can't be prefetched by adding another hint: its address has to be discovered first, or a representation has to precompute a shortcut. Shortcuts change build cost, footprint and cache behaviour, and their full cost has to be counted.

items.title: Local and end-to-end objectives
items.text: For a phase taking fraction \(f\) of total time, speeding it up by \(s\) gives an idealised whole-program speedup of \(1 / ((1 - f) + f/s)\), if nothing else changes. In a concurrent decoder that condition matters: changing one phase can alter shared-memory pressure, scheduling and its overlap with other phases. Wall throughput and CPU cost can also diverge: four workers may finish sooner while using more CPU-seconds per GB, and a small CPU saving may barely change a saturated pipeline's elapsed time.

items.title: What remains unknown
items.text: The public article doesn't establish the exact 2022 binary and full runtime configuration, and its measured knee can't uniquely identify a hardware queue's capacity. For mibz2, the archived evidence doesn't yet divide the four-worker penalty among LLC capacity, request congestion, writeback interference, prefetch timing and translation; nor does the static address-port model alone establish the limiting resource of the unrolled candidate. These are bounded, testable uncertainties.
