items.title: Memory-level parallelism in mibz2
items.text:
mibz2 · Research blog

In June 2022 Daniel Lemire published Memory-level parallelism: Intel Ice Lake versus Amazon Graviton 3. His benchmark walks a large random array as a chain of dependent loads, then walks it as several independent chains at once, and reads the speedup as a measure of how many memory accesses a core can keep in flight.

Ivica Bogosavljevic replied that the speedup isn't only memory-level parallelism (MLP): by interleaving work, the benchmark also raises instruction-level parallelism (ILP), and a fuller account would report instructions per cycle, instruction counts and where the loads are served from. Denis Yaroshevskiy asked how large each read is. Lemire answered that the data is out of cache, that IPC is far below one, that the source is available, and that he welcomes criticism and better measures.

The question matters to mibz2 because its inverse-BWT decoder works the same way: it advances 32 independent traversals of one table so that their lookups overlap. Our recent work has looked closely at the instructions in that loop. So we want to know what such a speedup does and doesn't establish, and which measurements would tell the explanations apart.

One point first. Lemire isn't saying the benchmark can't be reviewed. In the replies below he says the source is fully available, that he is happy to receive criticism, and asks for an alternative measure. That is a defence of the benchmark's usefulness, not a claim that scrutiny is impossible. A reviewer can ask for supporting measurements without having to invent a replacement benchmark.

The exchange, June 2022

Screenshots of the replies to Lemire's post, cropped to remove the phone's interface. Top: Ivica Bogosavljevic, 8 June 2022, agreeing with the overall idea, arguing that interleaving raises ILP, and asking for IPC or CPI and instruction counts. Middle: his question about allocation and cache level, and Denis Yaroshevskiy's about read size, 8–9 June 2022. Bottom: Lemire's two-part reply and his clarification, 9 June 2022. Fuller context: first excerpt, second excerpt. Transcript of the screenshots

Ivica Bogosavljevic, 8 June 2022: I read the post, the overall idea of the post is good, but I think it misses a few important things to make the whole picture more clear:

Ivica Bogosavljevic, 8 June 2022: (1) You use the term memory-level parallelism, but the speedup you are getting are not only because of it, but because of instruction-level parallelism. When you interleaved additional work, you broke some hard instruction dependencies, …

Ivica Bogosavljevic, 8 June 2022: … increased ILP so an out-of-order CPU had more available ILP and could run more instructions per cycle. You wouldn't achieve the same thing on an in-order CPU.

Ivica Bogosavljevic, 8 June 2022: (2) You should have measured instruction per cycle or cycle per instruction metric to measure CPU efficiency. Also you should have measured instruction count as well.

Ivica Bogosavljevic, 8 June 2022: (3) The data structure is a linked list, but it is not clear how it was allocated. Are loads mostly hitting L1, L2 or LL cache?

Denis Yaroshevskiy, 9 June 2022: Following of this - how big is the read and does it matter how big is the read.

Daniel Lemire, 9 June 2022, 1:58: This is out of cache and the instructions per cycle is small (much less than one). Obviously it assumes a superscalar processor but that's a prerequisite for a core to have multiple loads in flight. The source code is fully available. 1/2

Daniel Lemire, 9 June 2022: The approach is now pretty much standard and is used by many people. I am certainly happy to receive criticism. If you have a reasonable alternative measure of a core's memory-level parallelism, please share. 2/2

Daniel Lemire, 9 June 2022: Note that the hard dependencies are memory loads… not instructions… the instructions are mostly just out-of-cache memory loads. Please refer to the post for link to source code.

Here is what the rest of this post finds:

  • ILP and MLP are connected mechanisms here. Treating them as rival explanations creates much of the apparent disagreement.
  • The benchmark is useful, but its saturation point isn't a direct measurement of a hardware queue's capacity.
  • Instruction count and IPC are valuable diagnostics, and neither is enough as an optimisation target.
  • Our repository already holds the experiment a superficial answer would recommend: a large cut in instructions helped an isolated inverse-BWT walk, but gave essentially no measured throughput gain in the registered four-worker decoder test.
  • Several similar-looking "MLP" numbers in our investigations measure different things. Their denominators matter.

The performance results below come from the cited experiments. This review adds no new native benchmark of mibz2; what it adds is source inspection, reconstruction and interpretation. A longer companion page holds the detailed methodology, counter definitions and the full source register.

items.title: Memory-level parallelism in mibz2: instructions, overlap and evidence
items.text:
What does interleaving independent pointer chases really demonstrate? A 2022 exchange about Daniel Lemire's benchmark, read against mibz2's inverse-BWT walk.

2 November 2026 · 33 min read · Research synthesis

items.title: 1. What the two sides are saying
items.text:
Lemire's position, approximately:

This loop spends most of its time waiting for dependent, long-latency memory loads. Giving it independent chains lets several requests overlap. Measuring the resulting throughput is a useful way to characterise memory-level parallelism.

Ivica's, approximately:

Interleaving changes the instruction dependency structure too. To understand the improvement, show instruction counts, IPC and where the loads are served from.

Both contain something important. The questionable step is treating "more ILP" and "more MLP" as separate contributions to the speedup. In this workload the causal sequence can be:

  1. The program exposes independent load instructions.
  2. The processor issues those loads before earlier ones finish.
  3. Several memory requests overlap.
  4. More useful traversals complete per second.

The instruction-level independence enables the memory-level overlap. Calling the first part ILP and the second MLP doesn't mean two separately measurable speedups have happened. Work on MLP studies exactly how the instruction window, scheduling, branches and other instruction-side limits determine how much memory concurrency a core can achieve (Chou, Fahs and Abraham, ISCA 2004).

Here is how we'd assess the specific claims in the screenshots:

Claim Assessment Interleaving increases available ILP. Yes. Independent loads are independent instructions. It "breaks" the hard dependencies. Imprecise: the dependencies within each chain remain. The program supplies independent chains alongside them. IPC and instruction count should be measured. Sensible. They help characterise the change, but don't by themselves prove its cause. Allocation and cache residency matter. Yes. A random workload hitting L2 and one going to DRAM can give very different curves. The dependencies are "memory loads, not instructions". Loose: loads are instructions. The useful distinction is whether the critical delay is a memory access or ordinary computation. Superscalar execution is a prerequisite for several outstanding loads. Too strong as a general statement about processors. An in-order processor can't benefit this way. Also too strong. It depends on the design and on the order of the instructions.

There is useful context on Ivica's side too. In a later article he shows interleaved memory-access code that executes more instructions and still runs faster (Johnny's Software Lab). His broader argument isn't "minimise instruction count at all costs"; it's that exposing parallelism can justify extra instructions.

items.title: Reviewing, reproducing and explaining are different questions
items.text:
Review: can we inspect the algorithm, source, measurement method and interpretation? Yes.

Historical reproduction: can we recreate the exact 2022 executable, machine state, page mappings, compiler output and run conditions? That needs more provenance than source code.

Causal attribution: does the observed speedup establish the mechanism claimed, and rule out plausible alternatives? That needs suitable measurements or interventions.

Open source helps a great deal, but it doesn't settle all three. A fair assessment: the benchmark is a legitimate way to characterise overlapping dependent traversals, and some of the stronger readings of its output need more evidence.

items.title: 2. Why one chain is slow and several help
items.text:
Consider:

for (size_t i = 0; i < count; ++i)
    p = next[p];

The next address depends on the value the current load returns:

current index → load next index → compute next address → load next index

An out-of-order CPU can't issue the next ordinary demand load until it knows that address. Register renaming can't remove a true producer–consumer dependency.

Now unroll the loop:

p = next[p];
p = next[p];
p = next[p];
p = next[p];

That may cut loop-control overhead. It doesn't make the four loads independent. Compare four states:

p0 = next[p0];
p1 = next[p1];
p2 = next[p2];
p3 = next[p3];

Each lane still has a serial dependency from round to round. Within a round, though, the four addresses can be available independently. That is the central transformation.

Unrolling one chain, and interleaving four

One chain, unrolled four timesp = next[p]p = next[p]p = next[p]p = next[p]Each load’s address is the value the load before it returned.Four chains, interleavedround 1round 2round 3lane 0p0 = next[p0]p0 = next[p0]p0 = next[p0]…lane 1p1 = next[p1]p1 = next[p1]p1 = next[p1]…lane 2p2 = next[p2]p2 = next[p2]p2 = next[p2]…lane 3p3 = next[p3]p3 = next[p3]p3 = next[p3]…Arrows join each lane’s rounds. No arrow joins one lane to another, so a round’s four addresses are known together. A dependency diagram, not a timing trace: an arrow means "needs the result of". Unrolling lays one chain's loads out in the source, but each still waits for the last. Interleaving gives each round four loads whose addresses are known together. Whether they actually overlap depends on the processor and the memory system, and four lanes don't mean four cache misses.

Two details matter for mibz2:

  • A chain of integer indices is a pointer chase for performance purposes. It doesn't need language-level pointers.
  • Independent traversal states can share one allocation. They don't need separately allocated lists.

So our inverse-BWT table belongs to this family of workloads.

items.title: Latency and throughput are different quantities
items.text:
Suppose, purely as an illustration, that a dependent access takes 80 ns, that each access needs a 64-byte line not yet in cache, and that nothing else limits it yet:

Configuration Aggregate completion rate Time per completed step One chain 12.5 million steps/s 80 ns Eight perfectly overlapping chains 100 million steps/s 10 ns

In the second case an individual request can still take 80 ns. Eight requests overlap, so one completes every 10 ns on average.

At 3 GHz, 80 ns is 240 cycles. If each useful step retires three instructions:

\[ \mathrm{IPC}_{\text{1 chain}} \approx \frac{3}{240} = 0.0125 \]

With ideal eight-way overlap:

\[ \mathrm{IPC}_{\text{8 chains}} \approx 0.1 \]

That's an eightfold speedup with IPC still far below one. So Lemire's "IPC is much less than one" is consistent with his reading. It doesn't establish that instruction execution contributes nothing, or that another bottleneck can't appear as concurrency grows.

items.title: Superscalar, out-of-order and nonblocking are distinct
items.text:
Property Meaning Superscalar issue More than one instruction can start in a cycle. Out-of-order issue A later ready instruction can start before an earlier one that isn't ready. Nonblocking memory machinery Another memory operation can progress while an earlier miss is unresolved.

A processor can issue one instruction per cycle and still keep several long-lived requests outstanding across many cycles. There are concrete counterexamples to the universal claims in the replies:

  • Berkeley's original Rocket paper describes a single-issue, in-order pipeline with a nonblocking data cache that supports MLP (Lee et al., ESSCIRC 2014).
  • Arm documents three outstanding data-cache misses on the in-order Cortex-A55, under particular pipeline-spacing conditions (Cortex-A55 Software Optimization Guide).

That doesn't mean an arbitrary in-order processor gets the same result as an aggressive out-of-order core. Software ordering matters more there: if a dependent use blocks progress before the next independent load is reached, the independence can't help. Out-of-order execution usually makes available independence much easier to exploit; it isn't what defines MLP.

items.title: 3. What the 2022 benchmark measures
items.text:
The original article reports approximately:

Reported quantity Ice Lake system Graviton 3 system Single-lane access time 90 ns 120 ns Peak implied bandwidth 12 GB/s 9 GB/s Described simultaneous loads about 25 about 19

The stated environment is Ubuntu 22.04, GCC 11 and 4 KiB pages. These are measurements of those configurations, not permanent limits attached to the processor names.

The public benchmark revision available before the article is lemire/testingmlp at 2356903. That establishes the historical public implementation. It doesn't prove the exact local checkout or command line used for the post.

items.title: The data structure is more specific than "a linked list"
items.text:
The historical default uses:

  • 33,554,432 uint64_t entries: 256 MiB;
  • a random permutation forming one long cycle, built with Sattolo's algorithm;
  • several traversal states starting at positions along that cycle;
  • a second array used during setup, outside the timed traversal.

So it is an array-index pointer chase with several states, not a list of separately allocated nodes. That matters for allocation, translation and cache-line sharing (benchmark source).

The generator emits a separate function for each lane count, with a local state variable for each lane. It keeps the total useful access count approximately fixed:

\[ H(K) = K\left\lfloor \frac{H}{K} \right\rfloor \]

Going from one lane to \(K\) lanes changes the schedule of roughly the same work; it doesn't do \(K\) times as much.

The historical timing takes the fastest of five wall-clock trials. The code doesn't collect instruction counts, actual CPU cycles, cache-source information, page walks or memory-controller traffic.

items.title: Its bandwidth is inferred, not measured DRAM traffic
items.text:
The program multiplies logical accesses by 64 bytes per access and divides by elapsed time. But the architectural load reads eight bytes. The 64-byte figure models a cache-line transfer per access, and actual traffic can differ:

  • a line may already be cached;
  • several logical accesses can touch the same line;
  • requests can merge;
  • prefetching can generate or anticipate traffic;
  • translation can add memory accesses of its own.

So the benchmark's bandwidth is an implied cache-line bandwidth under its model, not a measurement at the memory controller. Likewise, its multi-lane ns/hit is

\[ \frac{\text{elapsed time}}{\text{aggregate completed accesses}} \]

which is reciprocal aggregate throughput, not the service latency of one request.

items.title: Its saturation point needs interpretation
items.text:
The historical code looks for the point where another lane improves performance by less than about 1%. A flattening curve could come from:

  • a memory-request resource saturating;
  • too little instruction-window space;
  • load or address-generation throughput;
  • translation limits;
  • register spills as lanes are added;
  • longer service latency under load;
  • a bandwidth limit;
  • noise around the chosen threshold.

The benchmark is useful because it gives a reproducible workload and a revealing curve. The curve alone doesn't say which of these caused the plateau.

items.title: 4. Four different things called MLP
items.text:
This is probably the most important conceptual point for our own investigations.

Quantity What it asks Available software independence How many chains or tasks can advance independently? Hardware capacity How many entries does a particular queue or tracking structure have? Achieved occupancy How many qualifying requests are outstanding on average? Effective speedup or saturation knee How much faster does the workload run, or when does another lane stop helping?

A program can have 32 active lanes without keeping 32 requests outstanding. A ten-entry structure doesn't mean every measurement called "MLP" must peak at ten. An eightfold speedup doesn't prove that eight DRAM requests were outstanding on average. And two processors with the same measured occupancy can differ in throughput if their requests take different times to service.

items.title: Little's law connects them, under strict conditions
items.text:
For a consistently measured population of requests over a suitable interval:

\[ \overline{N} = \lambda \overline{W} \]

where \(\overline{N}\) is the average number of outstanding requests, \(\lambda\) the request completion rate and \(\overline{W}\) the average time a request is resident. If each matching request transfers a line of \(S\) bytes:

\[ \text{line bandwidth} \approx \frac{\overline{N} S}{\overline{W}} \]

The hard part isn't the algebra but choosing matching quantities. A retired load, a fill-buffer allocation, an L2-miss transaction and a DRAM read aren't necessarily the same population. Nor is the latency of a serial, lightly loaded chain necessarily the latency in a heavily loaded multi-chain test: queueing, where the line is found and prefetching can all change it.

Higher occupancy can mean more useful requests are overlapping. It can also mean the requests are taking longer.

items.title: Why the smallest queue size isn't the answer
items.text:
Suppose a request holds resource \(j\) for \(W_j\) seconds, the resource has \(Q_j\) entries, and each useful step needs \(m_j\) such requests. Then:

\[ R \le \frac{Q_j}{m_j W_j} \]

The time an entry is held matters as much as the number of entries. A small queue passed through quickly can sustain more throughput than a large one whose entries stay occupied.

Travis Downs makes this point in the earlier discussion of the same benchmark: the core, the uncore, the memory controller and the memory itself all affect the observed limit, and the page configuration changes it too.

items.title: Translation is part of the experiment
items.text:
A 256 MiB array occupies 65,536 pages at 4 KiB, or 128 pages at 2 MiB: radically different translation working sets. A TLB miss can need page-table accesses before the intended data access can go ahead. The historical README already warns about this.

The code's MADV_HUGEPAGE request and the article's statement that the test used small pages don't contradict each other. A huge-page request doesn't establish what backing the program got: Linux can fall back to ordinary pages, and the actual mapping has to be checked (Transparent Hugepage Support).

If the question is "how does this workload behave under the machine's normal configuration?", translation is part of the answer. If it's "what is the core's data-request capacity apart from translation?", translation needs to be controlled or measured separately.

items.title: The question about read size is legitimate too
items.text:
There are several granularities:

  1. the operand an instruction loads;
  2. the cache line transferred;
  3. the useful payload consumed;
  4. the page translated.

A four-byte lookup can need a 64-byte fill. A second nearby four-byte lookup may reuse that line. A wider load may cost no extra fill, or may cross a line boundary. So "bytes the instruction reads" and "bytes moved through memory" are different accounts. That distinction matters for our packed u32 navigation table.

items.title: 5. Why instructions matter, and when counting them misleads
items.text:
A simplified model:

\[ c_{\text{step}} \gtrsim \max\left( \frac{L_{\text{dep}}}{K},\ \frac{u}{P},\ \frac{b}{B} \right) \]

where \(L_{\text{dep}}\) is the recurrence latency in cycles, \(K\) the number of effective independent chains, \(u\) the execution work per useful step, \(P\) the sustainable execution rate, \(b\) the bytes transferred per useful step and \(B\) the sustainable bandwidth in bytes per cycle.

It's an optimistic aid to reasoning, not a calibrated model of a processor; real resource limits need more detail than a single \(P\). It does capture the transition that matters here. With one chain, \(L_{\text{dep}}/K\) may dominate, and removing bookkeeping that overlaps the wait may do little. Adding independence lowers that latency-limited floor, until instruction execution, address generation, traffic, translation or something else becomes the limit. At that point, cutting instructions can become very valuable.

items.title: Fewer instructions can help in several distinct ways
items.text:
An instruction change may:

  • shorten the dependency that produces the next address;
  • reduce load/store or address-generation pressure;
  • reduce front-end work;
  • reduce register pressure and spills;
  • fit more useful independent loads into the finite instruction window;
  • reduce branch or bookkeeping overhead;
  • change prefetch timing.

These are different mechanisms. The finite window is particularly relevant: even with many independent chains in the source, the processor has to reach their loads before its tracking resources fill. Removing intervening work can raise the MLP achieved without changing the memory hierarchy's physical capacity. This interaction is central to the ISCA MLP work and to Cimple, whose subject is exploiting instruction- and memory-level parallelism together.

items.title: IPC is a ratio, not a score
items.text:
Over the same interval:

\[ \mathrm{IPC} = \frac{I}{C} \qquad\text{and}\qquad \frac{C}{B} = \frac{I/B}{\mathrm{IPC}} \]

where \(B\) is useful output. A hypothetical change:

Version Instructions/byte IPC Cycles/byte A 12 3.0 4.0 B 8 2.5 3.2

Version B uses 20% fewer cycles per byte despite lower IPC. Conversely, extra easy work can raise IPC without raising useful throughput. The practical objective is closer to: minimise elapsed time or CPU cycles per useful row or output byte, under the conditions that matter. Instruction count and IPC explain parts of the result; neither substitutes for it.

A rule like "IPC below one means memory-bound, above one means instruction-bound" is too crude. Intel's and Arm's methodologies use several categories and follow-up measurements because one ratio can't establish the cause (Intel's top-down method).

items.title: Instructions aren't execution-resource demand
items.text:
One instruction can expand into several back-end operations, and fusion can change some of the accounting without removing all of the work. Two sequences with similar instruction counts can put very different demands on load ports, store machinery, address generation or the front end. So for our loop the useful questions are:

  • Which instructions delay the next table address?
  • Which consume the resource that currently limits us?
  • Which make memory accesses just to maintain lane state?
  • Which occupy the window while more useful loads wait to become visible?

Those discriminate better than "can I remove three instructions?"

items.title: Normalise memory events to useful work too
items.text: Misses per thousand instructions can mislead during an instruction optimisation. Halve the instructions while misses per output byte stay the same, and MPKI doubles: the memory work per useful byte hasn't changed. We track misses and requests per BWT row or per final output byte alongside instruction-normalised figures.

items.title: 6. What mibz2's walk does
items.text:
The source examined for this review is master at 13e9854. The README still describes an earlier 12-lane, 256-start configuration; the current Segmented path dispatches to the room walk, with 32 lanes, 512 candidate starts and PF_L1 prefetching. Starts are deduplicated, and blocks below 65,536 rows take the serial path (src/bwt.rs).

The ordinary step is approximately:

let q = t[lane.row];
lane.row = q >> 8;
prefetch(t, lane.row);
output_for_lane[offset] = q as u8;

This leaves out segment boundaries and the start flag, but captures the recurrence:

  1. Load the packed table entry.
  2. Extract the next row.
  3. Start fetching it.
  4. Emit the current byte.
  5. Work on other lanes before coming back.

The room arrangement batches output writes using known spare capacity and a shared offset, which avoids some per-byte pointer and capacity bookkeeping. The segments' outputs are then assembled in final traversal order.

The prefetch's lead time in the room walk

lane 0q = t[row]row = q >> 8prefetch(t, row)out[i] = q as u8lane 1its ownsteplane 2its ownsteplane 3its ownsteplane 0 againq = t[row]the prefetched rowthe prefetch’s lead time: the work on lanes 1 to 3order of execution, not to scale Execution order for four of the 32 lanes, with no durations. Once lane 0's entry arrives, its next row is known and the prefetch can start; the walk then serves the other lanes before coming back. That intervening work is the prefetch's lead time. If it's shorter than the memory latency, lane 0's next load still waits. The prefetch can't reach a second hop: that address isn't known until the next entry arrives.

items.title: Our table is very different from Lemire's array
items.text:
A full 900,000-row table of u32 entries is

\[ 900{,}000 \times 4 = 3{,}600{,}000 \text{ bytes} \]

That's 3.6 MB, against the historical benchmark's 256 MiB. On the i9 host in our records, it is much larger than the private L2 but can fit in the shared L3, depending on other live data and concurrent activity. A very large compressed input doesn't mean each table access goes to DRAM: the stage's active working set is what matters. MLP can still help for accesses served by the last-level cache or elsewhere beyond L1; we just need to say which boundary we mean.

items.title: The prefetch changes how to read the counters
items.text:
After q returns, the next row is known, and the prefetch can start that request while the program serves other lanes. It can't discover arbitrary future links: the one after that is still unknown until the next entry is read.

A prefetch can also leave the ordinary retirement path before its data arrives, which lets the program keep memory work ahead of demand while still being limited by address discovery, issue resources, translation and request queues. That has a consequence for measurement: a demand load that hits in cache may be consuming a line whose expensive retrieval a prefetch started earlier. Counting only demand loads that miss in L3 can leave out much of the expensive traffic the walk causes.

items.title: The BWT literature is directly relevant
items.text: Kärkkäinen, Kempa and Puglisi's Slashing the Time for BWT Inversion studies both reducing costly accesses and overlapping the work of several starting positions. It's a direct algorithmic antecedent of our problem, not an analogy with hash tables or trees. It also points to two separate axes: make the existing accesses overlap better, or change how much costly access work there is. It's worth keeping them apart when deciding what an instruction optimisation is meant to achieve.

items.title: 7. Our unrolling experiment
items.text: A generic answer might advise exposing more lanes or unrolling the loop. Our records already go well beyond that.

items.title: The 8.6 figure is a throughput factor
items.text:
The October 31 post compares 38.55 cycles per byte for one chain with 4.49 for the room walk:

\[ 38.55 / 4.49 \approx 8.59 \]

That is a throughput ratio under that experiment's timing conventions, not a count of outstanding requests, as the post itself says. A model assuming unchanged latency can turn such a ratio into "effective chains", but prefetching, different instruction costs and changed service conditions make that an approximation. All 32 lanes can do useful work even if only some of them have a request outstanding at a given boundary at any instant.

items.title: Then we cut the instruction stream substantially
items.text:
The archived assembly comparison reports approximately:

Static hot path, per ordinary lane step Original Unrolled Instructions 16.4 10.44 Loads 3.0 3.06 Stores 2.03 2.16 Prefetches 1 1

The function grew to about 30 KB. These are static hot-path counts, not dynamic whole-decoder instructions per output byte. They show that much bookkeeping disappeared while the demand for memory operations didn't fall (assembly-fidelity analysis).

On the recorded EPYC 7763 stage test, the time ratio of the unrolled walk to the original was

\[ 0.877 \quad [0.863,\ 0.891] \]

about a 12.3% time reduction, or roughly 14% more throughput at the point estimate. So an instruction-stream transformation did materially help the isolated stage in that experiment.

items.title: The target-machine decoder result was much smaller
items.text:
The registered full-decoder test on the i9-10900K reported:

Configuration Throughput, unrolled ÷ original Interval One worker 1.017 1.006–1.028 Four workers 1.000 0.987–1.012

A control workload's CPU cost regressed. The registered verdict was negative, and the decoder-level experiment was archived (full-decoder results).

This bears directly on the 2022 exchange: cutting instructions can improve a local implementation and give little or nothing under the conditions that matter for the product. The stage and full-decoder tests also ran on different processors, so together they aren't a controlled measurement of one architectural variable.

items.title: What is established, and what is still a hypothesis
items.text:
Established:

  • the transformation substantially cut the static instruction stream;
  • it improved the recorded isolated stage;
  • the registered four-worker decoder test showed no throughput improvement at the point estimate.

Not established:

  • that total instruction count alone caused the isolated gain;
  • that address-generation pressure caused the target-machine result;
  • that memory bandwidth alone erased the gain;
  • that the larger code caused a regression.

The archive proposes load and address-port pressure on Comet Lake as a plausible explanation, and labels it a static model, which is the right status. The stronger next question is: which resource reduction would help under the target conditions, beyond cutting bookkeeping that may already overlap other work?

items.title: 8. One worker against four
items.text:
The corrected decoder-attribution analysis gives approximately these arithmetic means:

Quantity One worker Four workers Retired instructions per final output byte 32.63 33.06 CPU cycles per final output byte 13.46 17.51 IPC, derived 2.42 1.89 CPU-seconds per GB 2.707 3.579 Effective frequency about 4.97 GHz about 4.89 GHz

Retired work rises about 1.3%, cycle cost about 30% and CPU time about 32%. That makes a large rise in retired instruction work a poor explanation of the efficiency loss: almost the same retired work is taking substantially more cycles. It doesn't identify the cause, since cache behaviour, request service time, speculation, synchronisation and the mix of phases can all matter, but it narrows the search.

Both IPC values are above one, which shows again why an IPC threshold can't declare a workload instruction-bound. And four workers can raise aggregate wall-clock throughput while worsening CPU-seconds per GB: those are different objectives.

items.title: The stage boundary matters
items.text:
The corrected proposal separates two results:

  • on 197 matched full-sized blocks, traversal plus assembly rises from 1.234 to 1.806 CPU ns per BWT row;
  • across all 434 blocks, that interval adds about 0.61 CPU-seconds per GB of final decoded output.

These are different populations and denominators. The old trace also combines traversal and assembly, so blaming the whole increase on pointer chasing would overstate it.

items.title: Cache-capacity explanations need arithmetic and controls
items.text: Four maximum-sized tables occupy 14.4 MB before any other buffer. The host has a 20 MiB L3, and the trace estimates fewer than four live tables on average. So "four workers necessarily overflow L3 with their tables" isn't established; other live data, write traffic, replacement behaviour and queueing can still make shared-memory interference important. And the trace's association between longer walks and more overlapping walks is suggestive, not conclusive, because a longer interval has more opportunity to overlap another. That's one reason controlled interference experiments are useful, as the previous post describes.

items.title: 9. Counters and their denominators
items.text:
This is where we'd spend the most care in future analysis. Let:

  • \(O\) be an occupancy counter that adds the number of qualifying outstanding requests each cycle;
  • \(A\) the number of matching requests;
  • \(P\) the cycles with at least one matching request outstanding;
  • \(C\) all relevant cycles.
Ratio Units Meaning \(O/A\) cycles per request Average residence time \(O/P\) requests Average occupancy, given that a request is pending \(O/C\) requests Average occupancy over all measured cycles

One occupancy trace, three ratios

cycle 0cycle 1cycle 2cycle 3cycle 4cycle 5request Aoutstanding 3 cyclesrequest Boutstanding 3 cyclesoutstanding012210O = 6 request-cyclesA = 2 requestsP = 4 pending cyclesC = 6 cyclesO ÷ A = 3 cycles per requesthow long a request stays outstandingO ÷ P = 1.5 requestsoccupancy while anything is pendingO ÷ C = 1.0 requestoccupancy over the whole window A made-up trace, not mibz2 data. Two requests, each outstanding for three cycles, fall inside a six-cycle window, so no boundary correction is needed. The two idle cycles count in C but not in P, which is why O/P and O/C differ.

All three are useful, and they answer different questions. They are only valid if the numerator and denominator cover the same requests, interval, privilege filters and hardware scope, and short phase windows need care with requests already outstanding at the start or still outstanding at the end.

items.title: Why "MLP stayed at 2.18" settles nothing
items.text:
Intel's derived MLP metric is

L1D_PEND_MISS.PENDING / L1D_PEND_MISS.PENDING_CYCLES

which is conditional on cycles with a qualifying miss pending (event definitions, derived metrics). In our archive the conditional value stays around 2.18 while the fraction of cycles with a pending demand miss rises from about 12% to 30%. As an illustration:

\[ 2.18 \times 0.12 \approx 0.26 \qquad 2.18 \times 0.30 \approx 0.65 \]

So an unchanged conditional average can sit beside a large rise in occupancy over all cycles. The products are only illustrative; exact aggregation should use the matching raw totals. The point is the denominator. There's a further limit: these are process-wide measurements, so a change in how long the process spends in each phase also moves them. They aren't automatically measurements of the inverse-BWT walk alone.

items.title: The L1 event isn't "the number of independent BWT chains"
items.text: Intel's definition concerns demand-associated fill-buffer occupancy. A fill a prefetch started can begin to count once a demand access joins it, and page-walk reads and split accesses complicate the mapping to source-level loads. So this metric isn't the software lane count, total prefetch concurrency, the number of DRAM reads or the number of chains making progress. A lane count, a throughput ratio and this counter ratio should never be equated, and some of the values we have quoted come from different experiments and processors.

items.title: The offcore ratio is latency-like
items.text:
For the relevant Intel event family,

OFFCORE_REQUESTS_OUTSTANDING.ALL_DATA_RD / OFFCORE_REQUESTS.ALL_DATA_RD

has units of cycles per request. Its occupancy runs from an L2 miss until the transaction completes at the superqueue boundary, and its population includes demand and prefetch traffic and can include requests served by the LLC. It isn't automatically DRAM latency.

Our archived median rises from roughly 39 to 58 cycles per request (an arithmetic mean gives about 41 to 58). That's consistent with a longer average residence for the counted population. It doesn't prove that an unchanged set of useful BWT requests each became slower by that amount: the source mix, the phase mix and the request mix can all change.

items.title: Demand-only counts can't classify all the traffic
items.text:
Suppose a prefetch starts fetching a line. Later, a demand access either finds the line in L1 or joins the fill still in flight. The demand event describes the eventual demand access, not necessarily the whole history of the line. Likewise, MEM_LOAD_RETIRED.FB_HIT records a load joining an existing fill; the request that started it could have been a demand or a prefetch. It isn't a "prefetch supplied this fraction" counter.

That's why the corrected proposal withdraws two earlier readings:

  1. the estimate that about 98% of walk traffic was prefetch, which came from comparing unlike event populations;
  2. treating an inferred value of around six outstanding requests as directly measured, constant walk MLP. That figure combined an assumed number of requests per row, mixed process-wide residence data and stage timing, and their agreement was partly built in by the assumptions.

items.title: Aggregating workers adds another distinction
items.text: Summing occupancy counts and cycle counts across threads, then dividing, gives a cycle-weighted average per logical processor. It doesn't give the total number of requests outstanding at once across the machine. An unweighted average of per-thread ratios, on the other hand, can give short-lived or lightly loaded threads too much weight. Counter arithmetic is part of the definition of the measurement, not a last step in a spreadsheet.

items.title: 10. What the next experiment needs to distinguish
items.text: Our work is already past "try more lanes and see whether it gets faster". The next experiments should tell specific explanations apart.

items.title: Choose the objective explicitly
items.text: For the production decoder: wall-clock decoded throughput, CPU-seconds per GB, behaviour across blocks, and memory footprint. For understanding the walk: actual cycles per BWT row, nanoseconds per row, and requests, instructions and traffic per row. A stage improvement and a decoder improvement are separate results, and both are worth recording.

items.title: Isolate the phases without losing production behaviour
items.text: Measure table construction, traversal, segment assembly and the later output processing separately, and keep the whole-decoder test. Use the production sequence of blocks and buffer lifetimes: a prebuilt table traversed over and over can be much warmer than one met during real decoding, and the surrounding phases may be what creates the shared-memory conditions that slow the production walk.

items.title: Keep the axes separate
items.text:
These are distinct changes:

  • more lanes within one core;
  • more segment starts;
  • a different prefetch policy;
  • more worker threads;
  • a different layout for lane state;
  • different output-buffer lifetimes.

More lanes try to improve overlap within a core. More workers add cores, and also add pressure on shared resources. Calling both "more parallelism" hides an important difference.

items.title: Collect a small set of phase-matched measurements
items.text:
Measurement What it helps answer Actual cycles and ns per BWT row Did useful service improve, and did the frequency change? Retired instructions per row Did dynamic instruction work fall? Branch misses per row Did recovery costs change? Load/store and resource-pressure evidence Did the change reduce the resource that matters? Requests and supplier information per row How much counted traffic is there, and where is it served? Conditional occupancy How many requests overlap when any is pending? Pending-cycle fraction and unconditional occupancy How much of the time is that activity going on? Matching residence-time estimate Are requests taking longer to finish? Whole-decoder throughput and CPU cost Does the change improve the actual program?

No single row is a verdict. The combination should support or contradict a prediction.

items.title: Write the predictions before reading the results
items.text:
Hypothesis Result that would support it Too few independent loads become visible Better scheduling raises the useful request rate and cuts stage time, without extra traffic. Lane bookkeeping consumes a limiting resource A controlled layout or instruction change reduces that resource and the native stage cycles, with similar request behaviour. Translation is significant Verified mapping changes move page-walk activity and stage time together. LLC residency deteriorates Supplier and replacement evidence changes with a controlled live footprint. Shared request service is congested Residence time and slowdown respond to request pressure even with the footprint controlled. Output traffic interferes with traversal A targeted change to output lifetime or write traffic improves the affected stage and the production decoder.

None of these interventions is pure. Changing instructions changes request timing; changing page size can change placement; changing traffic changes queueing. The experiment should record those consequences rather than assume them away.

items.title: Respect what the existing harnesses measure
items.text:
examples/sweep.rs already explores lane counts, prefetch hints and walker variants, keeps decode order, and has an optional separate PMU pass. Two normalisations need keeping in view:

  • the sweep's byte denominator is BWT rows, while examples/phases.rs uses final decoded output;
  • both report c/B by converting elapsed seconds with a supplied nominal clock, which isn't an actual CPU-cycle count.

A fixed nominal multiplier cancels in a time ratio, so comparisons remain useful. Those values just shouldn't be mixed with PMU cycles, or across different byte definitions.

items.title: Use counters in small, meaningful groups
items.text:
For phase measurements, use matching intervals and filters, keep the enabled and running times, and quantify the instrumentation's own cost. Avoid collecting so many events at once that multiplexing makes short, changing phases hard to read. If you take interval deltas with perf_event_open, handle the time-accounting baselines as well as the counter baselines: resetting the counts doesn't reset all the timing metadata (perf-stat, perf_event_open).

The next experiment should fill a specific gap, such as phase-specific request populations or actual traversal cycles, rather than reopen the already-negative unrolling experiment without a new hypothesis.

items.title: 11. What the tools can and can't establish
items.text:
Disassembly is essential for instruction questions. It shows whether independent loads stay visible, whether lane state is reloaded, whether bounds checks or spills remain, whether the intended simplification happened, and where code grew. It can't show the cache residency or service time a run experiences. Keep the binary that produced the measured result: a small source change can alter register allocation well beyond the lines you meant to change.

LLVM-MCA helps investigate dependencies and execution-resource pressure. Its documentation limits its memory model explicitly: it doesn't predict a workload's actual cache behaviour, and its default load latencies are optimistic (llvm-mca). "This sequence creates address-port pressure under this model" can be useful. "This proves the production walk has reached its real MLP limit" isn't justified, and neither is "this proves the prefetch arrives in time". Treat it as a source of candidate explanations and lower bounds.

Cachegrind's reproducible instruction counts make instruction regressions easier to catch, but its manual cautions that the cache and branch simulations are basic (Cachegrind). A deterministic instruction-count improvement is real evidence of less work executed under that tool. It isn't a measurement of native out-of-order overlap, prefetch timeliness or contention.

Hardware counters observe defined events; they don't label causes. The CPU model, the event definition, filtering and errata all matter, and Intel and Arm events with similar names needn't count equivalent things. For Neoverse V1, Arm's own performance-analysis methodology is the right reference, not Intel's formulas. And stall events can overlap, so several of them can't simply be added into an exclusive account of elapsed time.

items.title: 12. Where this leaves the instruction work
items.text:
Keep inspecting instructions: our evidence supports it. The isolated unrolling result shows that changing the instruction stream can materially improve the walk. But the evidence also supports a more specific objective than cutting instruction count:

Find the dependency or resource that limits useful rows per cycle under the production workload, then change the instructions, state layout or memory traffic that consume it.

For the four-worker decoder, the strongest current observation is that roughly the same retired work takes substantially more cycles. The open task is to attribute that increase across traversal, assembly, request service and the interaction with the other workers.

Lemire's benchmark explains why independently advancing chains are valuable. It doesn't give us a universal concurrency number to aim for, prove that our 32-lane walker is saturated for the same reason, or settle whether the next profitable change is in bookkeeping, address generation, cache behaviour or traffic. Our own controlled results and their corrections are now the more specific evidence. The next step is to make those measurements phase-specific and consistent in their populations, with the complete decoder still the test of whether an optimisation earns its place.

items.title: Further reading
items.text:
Slashing the Time for BWT Inversion, Kärkkäinen, Kempa and Puglisi, DCC 2012. Start here for the algorithm itself: it covers reducing costly accesses and overlapping inversions from several starting positions, which helps separate how much expensive work there is from how it's scheduled.

Microarchitecture Optimizations for Exploiting Memory-Level Parallelism, Chou, Fahs and Abraham, ISCA 2004. Why finite instruction windows, execution structure, branches and other microarchitectural limits bound the memory overlap a core can expose: a firmer basis than treating MLP as a cache parameter.

Asynchronous Memory Access Chaining, Kocberber, Falsafi and Grot, PVLDB 2015. Suspended memory-bound tasks, uneven progress and the cost of scheduling them: the trade-off between keeping useful requests in flight and paying to manage their state. Its speedups aren't predictions for BWT.

Cimple: Instruction and Memory Level Parallelism, Kiriansky et al., PACT 2018. The clearest treatment of ILP and MLP as working together rather than as competing explanations, including the limits from intervening instructions and execution windows.

Travis Downs on the earlier benchmark. The measurement complications for this same benchmark family: several resources along the path, different occupancy times, and translation.

Intel's event and metric definitions. For the i9 investigations, the authority on what each ratio counts. Reading the exact numerator and denominator is worth more than any secondary article's name for a metric.

Research records: Measurement notes and source register · Unrolled walk: assembly comparison · Unrolled walk: i9 full-decoder results · Decoder attribution on the i9 · Inverse-BWT memory proposal, with corrections.

items.title: Concepts
items.text:
mibz2 decodes bzip2 as libbzip2 1.0.8 defines it, byte for byte, with every check libbzip2 makes, and decodes several blocks at once.

  • Why 32 couriers beat one: memory-level parallelism, the decoder's premise. One courier waits at every stop to learn the next address; 32 couriers' waits overlap. The lanes, the prefetch, the per-step cost that binds next, and the measurements.
  • What is checked, and when: block CRCs, stream CRCs, what an error reports, and the four inputs mibz2 refuses where libbzip2 does not.
  • How it works: the one sequential phase (the scanner), the workers, and the inverse BWT walked as 32 interleaved chains.
  • Prior work: libbzip2; Kärkkäinen, Kempa and Puglisi (DCC 2012); lbzip2 and pbzip2.

items.title: Block CRCs, before the block's bytes
items.text: Every block's CRC is checked before any of that block's bytes are returned. A block whose CRC does not match returns none of its bytes: the error comes instead. The bytes returned before an error are exactly the stream's up to the bad block.

items.title: Stream CRCs, at the stream's end
items.text:
Each stream's combined CRC is checked at the stream's end. The bytes of a stream's blocks are returned as each block is verified, before the stream's own CRC has been read. So a streaming caller has the whole stream verified only once a read reaches its end without an error: until then, what it has read is provisional.

In Python, BZ2Reader.verified turns true only when a read returns the end with every block's and stream's CRC matched.

items.title: Where an error was found
items.text:
An error says where decoding failed: in Rust Error { kind, block, bit }, in Python the DecodeError message. That is which block, and the bit it starts at. A damaged bit can be found later than where it lies, since the input is only known to be wrong once something it encodes fails a check.

The error kinds (ErrorKind):

  • the input: Empty, NotBz2, Truncated, TrailingData;
  • each of libbzip2's block checks: BadBlockMagic, BadOrigPtr, NoSymbols, BadGroups, BadSelectors, BadSelector, BadCodeLength, BadHuffmanCode, SelectorOverrun, RunTooLong, BlockTooLong, RunUnfinished;
  • BlockCrc and StreamCrc, with the stored and computed values;
  • this decoder's refusals: Randomised, BlockTooLarge;
  • Io (from a BzReader's source), RangeOvershoot, Cancelled, and Internal (a caught panic: a bug).

items.title: What is decoded, and what is refused
items.text:
The format is libbzip2 1.0.8's, with every check it makes: bzip2 1.0 and later output. Four choices differ from it, and each has its own error:

input libbzip2 mibz2 randomised blocks (written only by bzip2 0.9.0 and earlier, before 1999) decoded refused (Randomised) bytes after the last stream that do not begin another stream ignored an error (TrailingData): nothing after a stream is silently dropped an oversubscribed Huffman code pointing past the alphabet a stale table entry read an error a block whose compressed form passes 64 MiB (a real block is at most about 4.2 MB) decoded an error (BlockTooLarge)

items.title: Why 32 couriers beat one: understanding memory-level parallelism
items.text:
Most of a bzip2 decode is one loop, the inverse Burrows–Wheeler transform's walk, and that loop spends most of its time waiting for memory. mibz2 doesn't make memory any faster. It keeps many of the walk's memory requests in flight at once, so the waits overlap. That is memory-level parallelism (MLP), and it is the library's basic premise.

This page explains it with couriers and a dispatcher, then gives the mechanism behind each part of the picture, and the measurements so far. How it works has the threads around the walk, and Prior work the work it builds on.

items.title: One courier, one chain
items.text:
A motorcycle courier learns each delivery address only on arriving at the previous one: open the envelope, read the next address. The third destination can't be known before reaching the second. The bike is fast, but most of the time goes on waiting to find out where to go next.

That is the ordinary inverse BWT:

  • The table. After Huffman decoding and move-to-front, a block's last column becomes the T-vector: one 32-bit entry a row, holding the row's byte (bits 0–7) and the next row (the bits above). A block holds up to 900,000 bytes, so the table is up to 3.6 MB, larger than most cores' L2 cache.
  • The walk. Start at the block's primary index. Each step loads the current row's entry, writes its byte, and takes the next row from the same entry. The next row is anywhere in the table, so the load usually misses the cache.
  • The wait. The step after can't start until that load returns, because its address is in the load's result. A chain of dependent loads keeps one miss in flight, and the core idles through each one.
courier 1the corewaiting for the next address (a cache miss)idle: nothing to do until the address comes backa steptime → One courier. Each step (dark) is a few instructions; most of the time goes on waiting for the next address (light). Schematic, not to scale.

The walk was measured as latency-bound directly, on the machine where mibz2's prototype was built: walking 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16 independent chains through one block, the cost fell from 28.5 to 4.4 cycles a byte of output (compute frontier, section 2). Memory bandwidth was nowhere near its limit. The walk was waiting, not moving data. libbzip2 and lbzip2 walk the one chain.

items.title: 32 couriers, 32 independent journeys
items.text:
Give each of 32 couriers a different delivery chain. While courier 1 waits for its next address, couriers 2, 3, 4… make progress. That is memory-level parallelism: the couriers don't travel faster, but there are enough independent journeys that waiting on one doesn't stop the rest. One courier is limited by the time it takes to get each new address; 32 keep many requests in flight.

courier 1courier 2courier 3courier 4the coreslots for couriers 5 to 32each courier's step, one after anothertime → Four of mibz2's 32 couriers. Each still waits as long for its address, but the waits overlap, and the core takes the other couriers' steps in the gaps. Schematic, not to scale.

The correction that keeps the picture faithful

The CPU doesn't employ 32 workers, and the lanes aren't threads. One core interleaves the instructions of 32 traversal chains, and its out-of-order machinery overlaps their memory requests. The better image is one dispatch centre managing 32 motorcycles, each getting its next destination only when its last delivery returns an address.

What counts is deliveries a second for the whole centre, not how fast one bike finishes its route: sustained throughput, not the latency of any one load. Every load still takes as long as before.

Several threads are several dispatch centres, one a block: mibz2's workers decode whole blocks in parallel (How it works). The lanes are the parallelism inside each one.

items.title: Where the independent journeys come from
items.text:
A block has one chain, not 32: the T-vector is a single cycle through every row (or, for a periodic text, a few). bzip2 carries no metadata to start a walk anywhere but the primary index. mibz2 makes the journeys itself:

  • Random starts. 511 pseudo-random rows, plus the walk's own first row, become segment starts. A random row is a random position in the text, so the cycle is cut into 512 segments of about equal length. (Evenly spaced rows clustered in the text and stalled the lanes.)
  • Flagged starts end a segment. Each start is flagged in bit 31 of its own T-vector entry, which links never use. A lane that reads a flagged entry has run into the next segment's start: its segment ends there, recording which start it ran into, and the lane takes the next unwalked segment.
  • 32 lanes walk in lockstep. Each round, every lane takes one step, writing its byte into its own segment's buffer.
  • The segments are stitched together afterwards. From the first row's segment, each segment is followed by the one it ran into, until the block's length is reached. The output is exactly the plain walk's, byte for byte, including a periodic block's several cycles. The flags are cleared before the walk returns.
  • Short blocks walk plainly. Under 64 KiB, the segments' bookkeeping costs more than the waits it hides; only a stream's last block is ever that short.
one chaincut at startsjoinedthe plain walk: one courier, row after row, from the primary index to the block's endA · lane 1B · lane 3C · lane 2D · lane 4E · lane 2F · lane 1G · lane 4H · lane 3▼ a start row, flagged in its own entry: the segment before it ends there, and a lane takes the nextA, then the segment A ran into (B), then C… until the block's length: exactly the plain walk's bytes One chain cut at flagged starts into segments, walked by four lanes in whatever order the lanes take them, then joined in order. mibz2 cuts each block into 512 segments for 32 lanes.

items.title: Prefetching: phoning ahead
items.text:
Lanes alone weren't enough. Without help, a lane's next load is issued only when its instructions enter the core's reorder buffer, which is full of the other lanes' steps. So the misses in flight were bounded by how many steps that window holds, and adding lanes didn't add misses.

mibz2 issues a software prefetch of each lane's next entry as soon as its row is known (prefetcht0 on x86-64, prfm pldl1keep on aarch64). A prefetch retires without waiting for its data, so every lane's miss starts at once. In the picture, the dispatcher phones each request through the moment an address is read, rather than when that courier's turn comes round on the board.

Try the counts yourself in this schematic. It has one dispatcher, whose paperwork for a step takes a tick or two, and each address takes 31 ticks to come back. The timings are made up for the picture.

The schematic needs JavaScript.

items.title: The dispatcher becomes the bottleneck
items.text:
There is only so much road, and one dispatcher. Add enough couriers and every wait is covered. Then the limit is the dispatcher: each step's paperwork, done for each courier in turn. Add more couriers past that point and the dispatcher spends more on coordination than the extra journeys earn.

In the core, the dispatcher's limits are these:

  • Instructions a step. Every lane's step is a handful of instructions: the load, the flag test, the byte's store, the write pointer's advance, the buffer-end check, the prefetch. With the misses overlapped, the walk runs at the rate the core can issue those instructions.
  • Register pressure. One lane's state (its row, its write pointers, its segment) fits in registers, but 32 lanes' state doesn't. It lives in the L1 cache, and every step loads and stores some of it.
  • Cache contention. The lanes' table lines, the 512 segments' buffers and the lanes' own state share the same caches. At four threads, four walks share the L3.
  • Outstanding misses. A core tracks only so many misses at once (its line fill buffers, and the L2's own queue). Beyond that, more lanes only queue.

The record shows both sides. Without the prefetch, 16 lanes were within noise of 12, and 24 or 32 were slower (PR #21). With it, 16 to 32 lanes were about 26–28% faster than 12 lanes without it, and within noise of each other at one walk. With four walks at once, 32 lanes won clearly. So mibz2 runs 32 lanes and 512 segments (the measured points).

It also explains why a cleverer-looking algorithm can lose. Once 32 misses are in flight, the walk is bound by instructions a step, not by the latency of each load. A change that saves steps but makes each one dearer loses. A change that keeps the steps and makes them cheaper wins.

items.title: Make the dispatcher efficient
items.text:
Once there are enough couriers, cut the paperwork a step. That's how the walk got faster:

  • The flagged walk (#12). It replaced the first segmented walk, which tested every step's row against a separate bitmap of the starts (12 lanes, 256 segments). The flag moved into the entry the step loads anyway, bytes went out through raw per-lane pointers instead of a growable vector's push, and the test for idle lanes left the hot loop.
  • The prefetch, with 32 lanes and 512 segments (#21): every lane's next miss starts at once, as above.
  • The shared-offset walk, after libsais's chain decode (#37, the default walk since 0.1.5). libsais 2.12's decode_chains runs room rounds of every chain at a shared output offset, where room is the fewest bytes any chain's buffer has spare. Within a pass, a lane's byte goes to its buffer's base plus the pass's offset, so the per-step pointer store and buffer-end test are gone. The lanes, the prefetch and the segments are unchanged, so the same misses are in flight. Only the instructions a step drop: one dispatcher's paperwork, done in batches.

Two cleverer-looking ideas from the literature were built, measured and dropped. Both changed the journeys themselves, and both lost to their extra cost a step:

  • The pair walk, ψ² (#34, after libsais and Kärkkäinen, Kempa and Puglisi's super-alphabet). Each entry holds the row two steps on, so the walk takes half the steps, two bytes at each. But each step costs about twice as much: the second byte comes from a first-byte lookup. With the prefetch keeping 32 misses in flight, halving the dependent loads bought almost nothing, and the pair table took about three times as long to build. Envelopes holding two addresses mean fewer stops, but twice the paperwork at each, and the envelopes take three times as long to fill.
  • Precopy (#36, after Kärkkäinen and Puglisi). Where a stretch of the walk repeats one already walked, its bytes are copied instead of walked. It copied 31.5% of the Wikidata blocks' bytes, and was slower all the same. The repeat check ran on every step, and the steps it skipped were the cheap ones, whose table lines were already in cache. The cost is in the scattered steps, which repeats never cover. A courier who checks the logbook for a repeated stretch at every stop loses more time than the short, nearby stretches it saves.
flagged walk (the default before #37): a step's journey, then its bookkeepingshared-offset walk (#37, the default): the same journeys, less bookkeeping a steppair walk, ψ² (#34, lost): two bytes a step, about twice the work a stepPrecopy (#36, lost): a repeat check on every step; the copies skip only cheap stepsthe journey: load the entry, take its bytebookkeeping: flags, pointers, buffer ends, checksa byte out The core's time once enough misses are in flight, schematically: the bytes out in the same time. The shared-offset walk keeps the journeys and cuts the bookkeeping. The pair walk halves the steps but doubles each one's work, and pays again in its build. Precopy adds a check to every step to skip a few cheap ones.

items.title: The picture, term by term
items.text: in the picture in the decoder a courier a lane: one traversal chain, walking one segment at a time a delivery address, read on arrival the next row, in the entry the step just loaded waiting for the address a cache miss on the T-vector a delivery chain a segment, from a flagged start row to the next start the dispatcher one core's instruction stream, interleaving all the lanes' steps the paperwork for each step the instructions a step: the flag test, the byte's store, the pointer and buffer bookkeeping phoning ahead the software prefetch of each lane's next entry the road, the board's size the core's limits: outstanding misses (line fill buffers), the reorder window, the caches deliveries a second for the centre bytes of output a second: throughput, not one load's latency several dispatch centres worker threads, one block each

items.title: Threads
items.text:
• The scanner. One thread reads each block's header and Huffman-coded symbols in order. This is the one sequential phase: a block's end is known only once its symbols are read. It finds blocks exactly, not by searching for the block magic, so a magic inside a block's data is never taken for a block. It is roughly a tenth of a decode on well-compressed text, more on poorly compressible data.
  • The workers. Each worker finishes a block: move-to-front, the T-vector, the inverse BWT walk, RLE1 and the CRC.
  • The reader takes the blocks in order. A block's error reaches the reader only once every block before it has been read.
  • Memory is bounded: at most slots blocks are in flight (by default twice the threads), and the buffers are reused from block to block.

With one thread, the same phases run in order on the calling thread.

items.title: The walk
items.text:
The inverse BWT is a chain of dependent loads: each step's row is the previous step's load. A plain walk keeps one load in flight. The default walk (bwt::walk_segments_room, the flagged walk in passes) keeps many, one a lane (Why 32 couriers beat one explains why, and where it stops paying):

  • 512 pseudo-random rows, the walk's first among them, are segment starts;
  • each start is flagged in its own T-vector entry, which ends the segment before it;
  • 32 lanes walk segments in lockstep, each taking the next segment when its own ends, and each lane's next entry is prefetched as soon as its row is known;
  • the lanes step in passes of room rounds, room the fewest bytes any lane's buffer has spare, each byte written at its lane's base plus the pass's offset, so a step has no pointer store or buffer-end test (after libsais's chain decode, #37);
  • the segments are joined in order.

It equals the plain walk on every list, lists of several cycles included: the join follows the segments' links until the block's length is reached. The flags are cleared before the walk returns. Blocks under 64 Ki are walked plainly. The kernel is behind bwt::InverseBwt (Segmented, the default; Plain), so a walk can be swapped and timed as part of the whole decoder.

items.title: Kernels
items.text: Kernels::detect() chooses at run time: AVX2 (with BMI1) for move-to-front and RLE1, and PCLMULQDQ for the CRC. Each has a scalar twin, used on any other CPU and on aarch64 (Kernels::scalar()). The walk's gain is scalar code, memory-level parallelism, so it holds on any CPU.

items.title: Prior work
items.text:
• The format and its checks are libbzip2's (Julian Seward, bzip2 1.0.8, decompress.c). mibz2 follows its decoding rules and makes each of its checks, in its terms. Its Huffman decode tables are built as BZ2_hbCreateDecodeTables builds them, so a stream libbzip2 refuses is refused here too. It is a separate implementation in Rust, not a port of libbzip2's code. The tests use libbzip2 itself (the bzip2 crate's bundled 1.0.8) as the oracle.
  • Interleaving several traversals of one BWT inversion on one thread, so that out-of-order execution keeps their loads in flight, is Kärkkäinen, Kempa and Puglisi's idea: "Slashing the Time for BWT Inversion", DCC 2012, pp. 99–108.
    • They also use a super-alphabet (an LF² table: two characters a dependent lookup) and "Precopy" for repetitive data. Neither is used here: both were built in mibz2 and lost (why).
    • What is particular here is only how the traversals are found in an existing bzip2 file, which carries no metadata for them: the random starts, the flagged starts that end each segment, and the joining in order.
  • libsais (Ilya Grebnov), 2.12's cyclic inverse BWT, "as used by bzip2": its RUN_LANES store, 16 equal last-column bytes linked at once, is in mibz2's T-vector build. Its chain decode's shared-offset passes are mibz2's walk since 0.1.5 (#37).
  • Block-parallel decoding is lbzip2's (Mikołaj Izdebski) and pbzip2's approach.
  • pbz2 (Soof Golan) arrived independently at a segmented, multi-chain walk too; the bake-off that found it is in the journals.

items.title: Python
items.text:
mibz2 needs Python 3.10 or later. It has no Python dependencies.

pip install mibz2

or with uv:

uv add mibz2

Wheels are built for Linux (x86-64, aarch64), macOS (x86-64, arm64) and Windows (x64). Each uses the stable ABI (abi3), so one wheel covers every Python version from 3.10.

items.title: Rust
items.text:
cargo add mibz2

The library depends on std only. Its minimum supported Rust version is 1.80. The python feature builds the Python extension module, and is only for maturin.

items.title: Python
items.text:
Write a .bz2 file with the standard library's bz2, to have one to read:

import bz2

with bz2.open("sample.bz2", "wb") as f:
    for i in range(10_000):
        f.write(f"line {i}\n".encode())

A whole file in memory, decoded on every CPU this process may use, or on one thread:

>>> import mibz2
>>> compressed = open("sample.bz2", "rb").read()
>>> data = mibz2.decompress(compressed)
>>> data == bz2.decompress(compressed)
True
>>> mibz2.decompress(compressed, threads=1) == data
True

A file read as it is decoded: open takes a path or a binary file object, and returns a buffered binary file. Its raw.verified turns true once a read has reached the end with every block's and stream's CRC matched:

>>> with mibz2.open("sample.bz2") as f:
...     first = f.readline()
...     before = f.raw.verified
...     rest = f.read()
...     after = f.raw.verified
>>> first, before, after
(b'line 0\n', False, True)

A bad input raises mibz2.DecodeError, a ValueError, from decompress or from the read at which it is found. The message says which block and bit decoding failed at:

>>> damaged = bytearray(compressed)
>>> damaged[len(damaged) // 2] ^= 0x10
>>> try:
...     mibz2.decompress(bytes(damaged))
... except mibz2.DecodeError as e:
...     print(type(e).__name__, isinstance(e, ValueError))
DecodeError True

items.title: Rust
items.text:
use std::io::Read;

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    // a whole .bz2 in memory (its streams one after another): on this thread, or on 4
    let data = std::fs::read("file.bz2")?;
    let text = mibz2::decode(&data)?;
    let same = mibz2::decode_parallel(&data, 4)?;
    assert_eq!(text, same);

    // any Read, as a Read: on this thread, or block-parallel on 4 worker threads
    let mut out = Vec::new();
    mibz2::BzReader::parallel(std::fs::File::open("file.bz2")?, 4).read_to_end(&mut out)?;
    Ok(())
}

A bad stream is an mibz2::Error (its kind, block and bit), or from a BzReader an io::Error of kind InvalidData wrapping it. The Rust reference lists the rest: the push decoder, the block scanner and the decoding of a range of blocks.

items.title: Building and testing
items.text:
The tools: a Rust toolchain, uv, just, and for the lints taplo, whitespace-format and cargo-machete.

just py         # maturin develop, then pytest
just test-ci    # cargo test and the doc tests
just clippy     # clippy on every target and feature, warnings as errors
just pc         # formatting and lints (as pre-commit runs them)
cargo test --release                                   # against libbzip2
cargo run --release --example fuzz -- 600 1            # a mutation fuzz loop, libbzip2 the oracle
cargo run --release --example bzcat -- 4 < f.bz2 > f   # the parallel decoder as a command

On aarch64: rustup target add aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu, apt install qemu-user gcc-aarch64-linux-gnu, then cargo test --release --target aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu --config .cargo/aarch64-qemu.toml.

The segmented walks' unsafe code also runs under Miri, on blocks small enough to interpret: cargo +nightly miri test --lib -- miri_ (about a minute; CI runs it on changes to src/bwt.rs). Those tests assert they reached the transitions the walks' handoffs guard (a buffer growing, a pass ending with a buffer full, a lane coming into the tail full, and so on), so a walk change that stops them reaching one fails rather than passing having checked less.

items.title: Benchmarking
items.text:
Performance is measured on CI (.github/workflows/bench.yml, the benchmark): a pull request that touches the decoder gets a comment with its head against its base. Locally, the same harness:

cargo build --release --example ab
target/release/examples/ab gen corpora 4
target/release/examples/ab run runs.jsonl --arms mibz2,pbz2,lbzip2 --threads 1,4 --rounds 5 corpora/*.bz2
target/release/examples/ab summary runs.jsonl

Where the parallel decoder's time goes as its thread count grows (#39) is measured by the occupancy instrument (examples/occupancy.rs, feature trace), run on the pinned Wikidata corpus by one recipe on any machine, as CI's Occupancy workflow does:

just bench-occupancy                             # 1, 2, 4, ... up to the CPUs allowed
just bench-occupancy --threads 1,2,4,8,12,16,20

It needs cargo, python3, git and lbzip2, and writes occupancy-<UTC time>.json: the machine as the process sees it, each thread count's throughput and the cost of tracing, and the decoder's own timeline (workers decoding or idle and why, the scanner, the reader, and per block its CPU time and run-queue wait). It is a diagnostic: the benchmark's paired A/B decides what is faster.

The benchmark has a version of its own (BENCH in bench/report.py), with its history in bench/CHANGELOG.md: - A pull request that changes the benchmark (bench/, examples/ab.rs, examples/phases.rs, .github/workflows/bench.yml) either adds a changelog entry with its new version, or says in its description why no version is needed. - A major version that redefines a family of figures adds itself to that family in MEANING (bench/report.py), so the site's history splits that family there and joins the others across it. - python3 bench/test_report.py checks that BENCH and the newest entry agree, and that the history joins versions but never runner models, core counts, corpora or a corpus's different contents.

items.text: .github/workflows/site.yml builds the site on every push to master, and after each Benchmark run on master, and publishes it to the gh-pages branch, served at https://lmmx.github.io/mibz2/. A pull request from this repository gets a preview under pr-preview/pr-<number>/, linked from a comment on the pull request and removed when it closes. items.title: Releasing
items.text: The crate and the Python package are released at one version, from one commit.

items.title: Deploy Release
items.text:
Run the Deploy Release workflow (deploy.yml) with a bump (patch, minor or major). It runs just release, which:

  1. bumps the version in pyproject.toml (uv version --bump) and sets the crate's in Cargo.toml to match;
  2. writes the crate's changelog with release-plz;
  3. commits chore(release): bump 🐍 -> vX.Y.Z and tags py-X.Y.Z;
  4. pushes the commit and the tag, then starts CI on the tag (a tag pushed with the workflow's token starts no workflow by itself).

CI on a py-* tag builds the wheels and the sdist and publishes them to PyPI, and publishes the crate to crates.io with release-plz (which tags mibz2-vX.Y.Z and makes the GitHub release). Both use Trusted Publishing, in the pypi and crates-io environments.

items.title: Out-of-band cases
items.text:
• Tag Release (tag.yml): tags an existing commit py-<version> at the version its pyproject.toml and Cargo.toml already hold (no bump), and starts CI on the tag. Each registry is skipped where it already has the version.
  • Release Notes (release-notes.yml): makes a version's GitHub release (v<version>) at a given commit if it does not exist, or updates its notes, from that version's section of CHANGELOG.md.
  • A wheel job that never got a runner (0.1.6: both macOS jobs were cancelled after 15 minutes waiting, so Release was skipped and PyPI had nothing while crates.io had the crate): re-run the failed jobs on the tag's own CI run. Release then uploads with --skip-existing. Don't bump, re-tag or republish. CI reports a runner that never came the same way as a failed build ("cancelled"/"failure"), so check whether the job's steps ran at all before treating it as a build failure.

items.title: Release notes: the evidence
items.text:
Every version's section of CHANGELOG.md is the GitHub release's notes, so it carries the release's evidence. release-plz writes a one-line entry per commit (and only for commits that touch the crate's files). After the release, rewrite the section by hand:

  1. Dispatch the tag-to-tag bench. Run Benchmark (bench.yml) from the Actions tab with Use workflow from the new tag and base the previous tag:

    gh workflow run bench.yml --ref vX.Y.Z -f base=vX.Y.W

    It is a paired A/B like a pull request's (the base's own harness binary as the arm mibz2@base/ab, the order alternating round to round), on one runner. Its figures are the run's summary and its artifact (bench-pr-<sha>: result.json, comment.md, runs.jsonl, stages.jsonl); nothing is recorded. The base needs examples/ab.rs, and the stage table needs examples/phases.rs (v0.1.2 on); v0.1.3 and v0.1.4 have run as bases this way. The comment's "the merge base with master" means the base given.

  2. Write the entry to the template below, from that run alone, in a pull request. Never add up or chain the pull requests' figures: they were measured against other bases, often on other runner CPUs. A section holds no line starting ## [ (Release Notes ends the section there), so its headings are ### and below.

  3. Re-run Release Notes (release-notes.yml) once the pull request is merged, with the version and its release commit, so the GitHub release takes the section from master.

items.title: mibz2
items.text:
mibz2: a fast bzip2 decoder, block-parallel and multi-chain within each block.

  • decompress: a whole .bz2 in memory, decoded.
  • open: a .bz2 file (a path or a binary file object) read as a buffered binary file, decoded as it is read.

Every block's CRC is checked before any of that block's bytes are returned, and each stream's combined CRC is checked at the stream's end. Bytes read from a stream before its end come from blocks whose own CRCs matched, but the stream as a whole is verified only when a read reaches its end: until then, treat what has been read as provisional (see BZ2Reader.verified).

open(
    source: Source, threads: int | None = None, buffer_size: int = 1 << 20
) -> BufferedReader[BZ2Reader]

Open a .bz2 file for reading, decoded as it is read.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default source Source

A path, or a binary file object open for reading.

required threads int | None

Decoding threads, as for BZ2Reader.

None buffer_size int

The buffered reader's buffer, in bytes.

1 << 20

Returns:

Type Description BufferedReader

A buffered binary file over a BZ2Reader (its raw), whose raw.verified says whether the whole input has been read and verified.

Examples:

>>> import bz2, mibz2, tempfile, os
>>> path = os.path.join(tempfile.mkdtemp(), "a.bz2")
>>> with bz2.open(path, "wb") as f:
...     _ = f.write(b"line one\nline two\n")
>>> with mibz2.open(path) as f:
...     lines = f.readlines()
...     verified = f.raw.verified
>>> lines, verified
([b'line one\n', b'line two\n'], True)
